concepts.in_practice: A team assigns one or two FDEs and an engagement lead per customer. In the first week they hold a kickoff, file every access and security request, and shadow the users whose work will change. They write a short solution document, agree the pilot criteria in writing, and then ship a thin end-to-end slice on real data within the first few weeks. A weekly status note goes to the sponsor, a shared channel handles daily questions, and an out-of-scope list absorbs new requests. After go-live the team writes runbooks, hands operation over, and files a field report that proposes which custom pieces should move into the product.

sources.title: What are Forward Deployed Engineers, and why are they so in demand?

body.body: The role was popularized by Palantir, where engineers were placed directly with customers to adapt a general platform to specific operational problems. It has since spread widely among AI companies, because model-based products rarely work out of the box on a customer's data and processes. An FDE writes production code, but the unit of success is a customer outcome, not a shipped feature. The engineer spends much of the week with customer users and operators, and the rest building integrations, data pipelines, prompts, evaluations and custom application surfaces.
body.heading: Definition and origin

body.body: A solutions engineer mostly works before the sale, demonstrating fit and answering technical questions. A professional services consultant configures and implements against a statement of work. A product engineer builds for many customers at once. The FDE overlaps all three but is distinguished by owning code in production for one customer and having direct influence on the product roadmap. Many companies pair the FDE with a deployment or engagement lead who owns the commercial relationship, so the engineer can concentrate on technical delivery.
body.heading: How it differs from neighboring roles

subtopics.title: What the forward deployed role is and where it sits

body.body: A typical engagement runs through six phases. Kickoff confirms the signed scope, stakeholders, success measures and access needs. Discovery maps the current workflow and the systems involved. Design produces a short solution document and an integration plan. Build delivers in thin vertical slices against real customer data as early as possible. Pilot runs the system with a limited user group against agreed criteria. Go-live widens the rollout, and handover transfers operation to the customer team or a support function, with runbooks, dashboards and an owner for each alert.
body.heading: Phases

body.body: The critical path is rarely the code. It is access: credentials, network allowlisting, security review, data sharing agreements and a sandbox that resembles production. Experienced FDEs request these on day one and track them as explicit dependencies with named customer owners. They also establish a weekly cadence with a written status note that states what shipped, what is blocked and what decision is needed, so that slippage is visible long before the go-live date.
body.heading: What usually blocks delivery

subtopics.title: The engagement lifecycle from signed scope to go-live

body.body: Shape Up describes shaped work as having three properties. It is rough: the description leaves room for the builder to make detailed decisions, unlike a pixel-level wireframe. It is solved: the main elements and how they connect are thought through, so the open questions are details and not the core approach. It is bounded: it states what is out of scope and how much time the work is worth. Applied to customer delivery, each milestone is written as a shaped pitch instead of a list of requested features.
body.heading: Rough, solved, bounded

body.body: Customers surface new needs as soon as they see working software. The default response is not yes or no but a placement decision: does it replace something inside the current boundary, go into a later phase, or become a product request? Keeping a visible out-of-scope list in the engagement document makes this routine. Fixing the time and letting scope vary protects the go-live date, which is usually the commitment the customer's sponsor cares about most.
body.heading: Handling new requests mid-engagement

subtopics.title: Shaping work so scope stays bounded

body.body: Anthropic's guidance on building agents separates workflows, where LLM calls and tools follow predefined code paths, from agents, where the model directs its own steps and tool use. The recommendation is to start with the simplest solution, often a single well-instrumented LLM call with retrieval, and add complexity only when measurement shows it helps. Agentic designs trade latency and cost for flexibility. In a customer deployment the simpler design is also easier to explain in a security review, easier to evaluate and easier to hand over.
body.heading: Workflows before agents

subtopics.title: Choosing the simplest AI design that meets the goal

body.body: The economic risk of the model is that every engagement becomes a one-off services project. The countermeasure is a deliberate loop: custom code is written in a separable layer, repeated patterns across two or three customers are flagged, and the product team absorbs them as configuration, connectors or platform features. FDEs write short field reports that describe the customer problem, the workaround built and the generalization proposed. Companies that run the model well measure how much of each new deployment is assembled from existing parts.
body.heading: From bespoke build to reusable capability

subtopics.title: Feeding field work back into the product

concepts.summary: A forward deployed engineer (FDE) is a software engineer embedded with a customer, responsible for making the product work on that customer's real data, systems and processes. The model trades some product-team leverage for speed and proximity: the engineer owns discovery, integration, custom build and go-live, then feeds what was learned back into the core product. This lesson lays out the engagement lifecycle, how scope is kept bounded, and why AI deployments favor the simplest design that meets the goal.
concepts.title: The forward deployed delivery model: from signed scope to go-live

concepts.in_practice: After discovery, the FDE writes a one-page scope and a short design doc in a shared document tool, with a C4 context and container diagram embedded. The customer's architect and security lead comment directly on the doc, and a review meeting resolves the open threads. Decisions that came out of the review are recorded as numbered ADR files in the engagement repository. Before build starts, the team walks the design through the quality pillars and records gaps as risks. The doc is updated when implementation diverges and is given to the customer's operating team at handover together with the ADR log.

sources.title: Architecture decision record (ADR) examples and templates

body.body: Scoping starts by restating the customer's problem in measurable terms, then listing constraints: data location, identity provider, network boundaries, compliance regime, latency budget, and who will operate the system. Each requirement is classified as must, should or out. The output is a one-page scope with goals, explicit non-goals, assumptions, dependencies on the customer, and the main risks. An FDE is expected to make most trade-off calls alone, so the discipline is to write each call down with its reasoning, so that it can be challenged later without relitigating from memory.
body.heading: From request to commitment

subtopics.title: Scoping an engagement and making trade-off calls

body.body: The format described for Google design docs is informal but consistent. Context and scope gives the reader the background facts briefly. Goals and non-goals lists what the system will do and what it deliberately will not. The design section presents an overview first, usually with a system-context diagram, then APIs, data storage and the degree of constraint the solution operates under. Alternatives considered explains why other reasonable designs were rejected. Cross-cutting concerns covers security, privacy and observability. The emphasis is on trade-offs, not on an implementation manual.
body.heading: Sections that matter

body.body: A design doc is worth writing when the solution is ambiguous, when senior review can catch an expensive mistake, or when several teams must agree. If the answer is obvious, skip it and prototype. For a customer engagement, a short doc of a few pages is usually enough, and it should be readable by the customer's architects. The lifecycle is draft and rapid iteration, review, implementation with updates as reality diverges, and a final pass so the doc remains an accurate entry point for whoever operates the system.
body.heading: When and how long

subtopics.title: The design document

body.body: An architecture decision record (ADR) captures a single significant decision in a short text file kept in the repository. The widely used template by Michael Nygard has a title, a status such as proposed, accepted or superseded, the context that forced the decision, the decision itself, and its consequences, including the negative ones. Records are numbered and never rewritten: a changed decision gets a new record that supersedes the old one. In customer work, ADRs are valuable at handover, because they explain why the system looks the way it does.
body.heading: One decision per record

subtopics.title: Architecture decision records

body.body: The C4 model gives four hierarchical diagram types. A system context diagram shows the system as one box with its users and the external systems it talks to. A container diagram opens that box into separately deployable or runnable units such as a web app, an API, a worker and a database. A component diagram shows the major building blocks inside one container. A code diagram shows classes and is rarely worth maintaining by hand. Supplementary views include system landscape, dynamic and deployment diagrams.
body.heading: Four levels of zoom

body.body: The context and container levels do most of the work. The context diagram is the one to show executives and security reviewers, because it makes every data flow across the customer boundary visible. The container diagram is what the customer's platform team needs to plan networking, identity and hosting. Each element should carry a name, a technology and a one-line responsibility, and every line should be labeled with what flows and over which protocol. A deployment diagram is added when the customer hosts the system.
body.heading: Use in customer engagements

subtopics.title: Drawing architecture with the C4 model

body.body: The AWS Well-Architected Framework organizes design review around six pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. Each pillar has design principles and questions. In a customer engagement the pillars work as a structured walkthrough of the proposed solution with the customer's architects: how is it deployed and observed, who can access what, what happens when a dependency fails, where are the latency and throughput limits, what does it cost per unit of work. Gaps become tracked risks with owners instead of surprises at security review.
body.heading: Pillars as a checklist

subtopics.title: Reviewing a design against quality pillars

concepts.summary: Scoping turns a customer's stated need into a bounded technical commitment, and the design document is where the trade-offs behind that commitment are written down and reviewed. This lesson covers the structure of a useful design doc, how to record individual decisions, how to draw architecture at the right level for each audience, and how to check a design against standard quality pillars.
concepts.title: Technical scoping, design docs and solution architecture for customer engagements

concepts.in_practice: The FDE spends several days shadowing operators and collects fifty to a few hundred real cases with their outcomes. The as-is process is drawn in BPMN with lanes per role and annotated with volume and handling time, then reviewed with the people who do the work until they agree it is accurate. The team scores each step, picks one or two candidates, and draws the to-be process with the model calls, the deterministic steps and the human review tasks made explicit. The first implementation is usually a fixed workflow with a review queue, built either in the vendor's own platform, in a tool such as n8n, or in code, and the collected cases become the first evaluation set.

sources.title: About the Business Process Model and Notation Specification 2.0

body.body: Managers describe the process as designed, and operators perform the process as it is. Discovery therefore combines stakeholder interviews with shadowing sessions where the engineer watches real cases being handled, including the spreadsheets, copy-paste steps and side-channel messages that no document mentions. For each step, record the trigger, the inputs, the system used, the decision made, the output and who receives it. Collect a sample of real cases, including the awkward ones, and baseline numbers such as volume, handling time, error rate and rework. Those numbers later become the success criteria.
body.heading: Observe, do not just interview

subtopics.title: Discovering the as-is workflow

body.body: Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) 2.0 is an OMG standard for process diagrams that both business and technical readers can follow. A small subset covers most needs. Events are circles: start, intermediate and end, often with a type such as message or timer. Activities are rounded rectangles: tasks, which can be typed as user, service or manual, and subprocesses. Gateways are diamonds that split or merge the flow: exclusive for one path, parallel for all paths. Sequence flows connect elements inside a participant, and message flows cross between participants.
body.heading: Core elements

body.body: A pool represents a participant such as the customer organization or an external supplier, and lanes inside it represent roles or systems. Laying the process out in lanes makes handoffs visible, and handoffs are where delay and errors concentrate. Keep the first diagram at the level a team lead would recognize, roughly ten to twenty activities, and model the happy path before exceptions. Then annotate each task with volume and time so the diagram doubles as the input to the automation decision.
body.heading: Pools, lanes and level of detail

subtopics.title: Writing the process down with BPMN

body.body: Score each step on value and feasibility. Value comes from volume, handling time, cost of delay and error cost. Feasibility depends on whether the inputs are available digitally, whether a correct output can be recognized and measured, how tolerant the step is of mistakes, and whether the action is reversible. Good first candidates are high-volume, text-heavy steps with a clear definition of done and a cheap way to catch errors, such as classification, extraction, drafting and summarization. Steps that are rule-based and deterministic belong in plain code, not in a model.
body.heading: Scoring candidate steps

body.body: Anthropic's guide describes a ladder of designs. The base is an LLM augmented with retrieval, tools and memory. Workflows compose calls on fixed paths: prompt chaining for sequential subtasks, routing to send inputs to specialized handling, parallelization for independent subtasks or voting, orchestrator-workers when subtasks cannot be predicted in advance, and evaluator-optimizer for iterative refinement. Agents, which plan their own steps in a loop, fit open-ended problems where the path cannot be hardcoded and the environment gives reliable feedback. Choose the lowest rung that meets the measured need.
body.heading: Matching the pattern to the step

subtopics.title: Choosing what to automate and with which AI pattern

body.body: In a mapped workflow, checkpoints are modeled as user tasks placed before irreversible or externally visible actions. Three design choices follow: what the reviewer sees, which should be the proposed action with its evidence and not raw model output; what happens on timeout or rejection, modeled as explicit paths; and how the gate relaxes over time, for example by auto-approving a class of cases once its measured accuracy holds above an agreed threshold for a sustained period. Reviewer decisions are logged as labeled evaluation data.
body.heading: Design choices beyond the gate itself

subtopics.title: Placing human checkpoints

body.body: Tools such as n8n model a workflow as a set of connected nodes: a trigger node starts a run from a webhook, schedule or application event, and action nodes call applications, transform data, branch or invoke a model. Each run is an execution that can be inspected step by step, which helps when debugging with customer staff. These tools suit integrations that the customer wants to own and modify. Use a code-based or durable workflow engine when the process needs long-running state, strict versioning, complex retries or rigorous testing.
body.heading: Low-code engines versus code

subtopics.title: Implementing the to-be workflow

concepts.summary: Before any model is called, an FDE has to understand how the customer's work is actually done and decide which steps are worth automating. This lesson covers process discovery, a notation for writing the process down, criteria for picking automation candidates and the right AI pattern for each, where humans stay in the loop, and how the result is implemented in a workflow tool.
concepts.title: Mapping customer workflows and choosing what to automate with AI

flowchart LR
  A[Charter: question, appetite, criteria] --> B[Prototype on real cases]
  B --> C[Log traces]
  C --> D[Expert review and labels]
  D --> E[Eval set grows]
  E --> F[Run evals on each change]
  F --> B
  F --> G{Criteria met by end date}
  G -->|yes| H[Pilot or production rollout]
  G -->|no| I[Stop or reshape]

concepts.in_practice: The team writes a one-page POC or pilot charter: the question, the appetite in weeks, the dataset, the criteria with thresholds, the decision owner and the next step on pass. The FDE builds a thin Streamlit or notebook front end over a pipeline function within days and demos on real customer cases. Every run is logged, a customer expert labels a sample each week, and failures are added to the evaluation set. A weekly readout shows the metrics against the thresholds and the baseline. At the end date the team presents results against the charter and the customer decides, instead of extending by default.

body.body: A prototype answers whether an idea is worth pursuing: it is built in hours or days, often on sample data, to make the concept concrete for stakeholders. A proof of concept answers whether it is technically feasible on this customer's data and systems, and it targets the riskiest assumption, such as extraction accuracy or an integration path. A pilot answers whether it delivers value in real use: a limited group of real users runs real cases over a few weeks, with production-grade access control, logging and support, even if scale and polish are limited.
body.heading: Three different questions

body.body: A POC without an agreed exit drifts into an open-ended free trial. Before starting, write down the decision it informs, who makes that decision, the date, the criteria, and what happens on pass: typically a paid pilot or production rollout with a named budget owner. Also agree what the customer must supply, such as data samples, a subject matter expert for labeling and access to a test environment. If these cannot be agreed, that is itself a signal about the engagement.
body.heading: Avoiding the stalled POC

subtopics.title: Prototype, POC and pilot: what each one proves

body.body: Anthropic's guidance on defining success asks for criteria that are specific about the task, measurable with a number or a well-defined qualitative scale, achievable given current model capability, and relevant to the application's purpose. A weak criterion is that the assistant should answer well. A strong one states the metric, the dataset and the threshold, for example an F1 score of at least a stated value on a held-out set of labeled customer cases. Most use cases need several dimensions at once: task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy preservation, latency and price.
body.heading: Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant

body.body: Criteria carry weight with a sponsor when they are expressed against the current process. Use the baseline from discovery: handling time per case, error or rework rate, backlog age, cost per case. A pilot criterion then reads as a comparison, such as median handling time reduced by a stated fraction with no increase in error rate on audited samples. Add guardrail criteria that must not regress, such as zero leakage of restricted fields, and agree who audits the samples and how disagreements are settled.
body.heading: Tying criteria to the baseline

subtopics.title: Writing measurable success criteria

body.body: Shape Up starts from appetite: decide how much time the problem is worth, then design a solution that fits, instead of estimating an imagined solution. Fixing time and varying scope forces trade-off decisions early. Two further habits apply directly to POCs. Narrow the problem by asking what specifically went wrong in the cases that prompted the request, which often reveals a much smaller target than the original ask. Watch for grab-bags, requests like a redesign or a general assistant with no single problem behind them, and decline to start until one concrete use case is chosen.
body.heading: Fixed time, variable scope

subtopics.title: Setting an appetite and narrowing the problem

body.body: For a prototype or POC, the interface only needs to let a stakeholder put in a real case and see the result with its evidence. Streamlit turns a plain Python script into an interactive web app: widgets such as text inputs, file uploaders and buttons are function calls, and the script reruns from top to bottom on each interaction, with session state and caching for anything that should persist. That keeps the engineer's time on the pipeline itself: data access, prompts, retrieval and output validation. Notebooks and simple chat front ends serve the same purpose.
body.heading: Thin UI over real logic

body.body: Decide at the start which parts are disposable. The UI usually is. The pipeline function, the prompt and schema definitions, the dataset of customer cases and the evaluation script are not, and should live in a repository with tests from the first day. Keep the pipeline behind a plain function or API boundary so the prototype UI can be replaced by the production surface without rewriting the logic. Log every input, output and intermediate step so that failures seen in demos become test cases.
body.heading: What to keep and what to throw away

subtopics.title: Building the prototype fast

body.body: Hamel Husain's framing has three levels: cheap assertion-style unit tests run on every change, human and model-graded review of logged traces on a regular cadence, and A/B testing once there are real users. In a pilot, the specific additions are that customer subject matter experts do the human review, so the trace viewer must be simple enough for them to use, and that the pass rate on the agreed dataset is reported to the sponsor each week as the evidence for the exit decision.
body.heading: Levels of evaluation in a customer pilot

subtopics.title: Running the evaluation loop during a pilot

concepts.summary: Prototypes, proofs of concept and pilots are how an FDE reduces uncertainty quickly and gives the customer evidence for a go or no-go decision. The work is only useful if the question being answered, the time allowed and the pass criteria are fixed before building starts. This lesson covers the distinction between the stages, how to write measurable criteria, how to bound the effort, and how to build and evaluate fast.
concepts.title: Rapid prototyping, POCs and pilots with measurable success criteria

modules.intro: This module covers how a forward deployed engineer takes a customer engagement from a signed scope to a system running in production, and the working methods that keep that delivery bounded and verifiable. It moves from the delivery model itself to scoping and design documents, workflow mapping, and proofs of concept with measurable exit criteria.
modules.title: Foundations: The Forward Deployed Delivery Model

code.code:
import asyncio, os
import httpx

BASE = os.environ["API_BASE"]

async def fetch(client, sem, rec_id):
    async with sem:
        r = await client.get(f"{BASE}/records/{rec_id}", timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()
        return r.json()

async def main(ids):
    sem = asyncio.Semaphore(8)
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        tasks = (fetch(client, sem, i) for i in ids)
        return await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True)

results = asyncio.run(main(range(100)))
print(sum(not isinstance(r, Exception) for r in results), "ok")

flowchart LR

  B --> C[Parse into typed models]
  C -->|valid| D[Transform]
  C -->|invalid| E[Reject file with reasons]
  D --> F[Load to target API or database]
  F --> G[Run report: in, out, rejected]
  E --> G

concepts.in_practice: A field team usually starts with a script in a shared repository that pulls a sample of the customer's data, parses it into typed models and prints a reject report, because that surfaces data problems on day one. Once the shape is understood, the same parsing code is lifted into a small FastAPI service or a scheduled job, with concurrency bounded to whatever the customer's API tolerates. Tests are written against captured real payloads with sensitive values scrubbed, type checking and linting run in CI, and the result ships as a container with a lock file so the customer's platform team can run it without asking questions.

body.body: Most field scripts follow one pattern: read records from a file or an API, normalize them, write them somewhere else, and report what was skipped. Use the standard library first: json, csv, pathlib, datetime, itertools and collections cover the majority of cases. Prefer generators so a large export streams row by row instead of loading into memory. Keep the transform a pure function from one record to one record, so it can be unit tested with a handful of literal dicts. Always count inputs, outputs and rejects, and write rejects to a separate file with the reason, because the customer will ask where the missing rows went.
body.heading: The shape of a good transformation script

subtopics.title: Scripts for parsing, reshaping and validating data

body.body: External payloads are untrusted even when the customer says the format is fixed. Define a model for each inbound shape and parse into it at the edge, so the rest of the code works with attributes that have known types rather than nested dict lookups. Pydantic coerces and validates in one step and produces an error that names the failing field, which is what you paste into a ticket for the customer's team. Use optional fields and defaults deliberately: a field that is missing, null, or an empty string are three different facts in a legacy export. Run a type checker such as mypy or pyright in CI so refactors stay safe.
body.heading: Parse, do not just check

subtopics.title: Typed models at the boundaries with Pydantic and type hints

body.body: asyncio runs many coroutines on one thread, switching between them only at await points. That fits integration work, which is mostly waiting on HTTP calls, databases and model APIs. A coroutine function is declared with async def and does nothing until it is awaited or scheduled as a task. asyncio.run starts the event loop, asyncio.gather or a TaskGroup runs several awaitables concurrently, and a Semaphore caps how many are in flight. Blocking calls freeze every other coroutine, so a synchronous client or heavy CPU work inside a coroutine must be moved off the loop with asyncio.to_thread or a process pool.
body.heading: The model

body.body: Unbounded gather over ten thousand records will exhaust a customer's rate limit or connection pool within seconds, so always bound concurrency and add a timeout to each call. Decide what one failure means: gather raises the first exception by default, while return_exceptions collects them so the batch can finish and report partial results. Cancellation is delivered as an exception at an await point, so cleanup belongs in try and finally blocks or async context managers. Retries need backoff and jitter, and the operation being retried must be idempotent or you will create duplicates downstream.
body.heading: What goes wrong in the field

subtopics.title: Concurrent I/O with asyncio

body.body: FastAPI maps a decorated function, called a path operation, to an HTTP method and path. Function parameters declare where data comes from: path parameters, query parameters, or a request body typed as a Pydantic model. The framework validates the request against those types, returns a structured error response when validation fails, and generates an OpenAPI schema with interactive documentation from the same declarations. Shared concerns such as database sessions, authentication and configuration are supplied through dependency injection with Depends, which also makes them easy to override in tests. The app runs under an ASGI server such as Uvicorn.
body.heading: How a FastAPI service is put together

body.body: The common shapes are a webhook receiver that validates and enqueues, a thin adapter that exposes a legacy system behind a clean JSON contract, and a backend for a pilot application that calls a model. Keep handlers thin: parse, call a plain function, return a response model. Declare a response model so internal fields never leak. Use async handlers when the work awaits I/O and plain def handlers when a library is blocking, since FastAPI runs those in a thread pool. The generated documentation doubles as the contract you hand to the customer's engineers.
body.heading: Typical field uses

subtopics.title: Small HTTP services with FastAPI

body.body: Code that runs on your laptop is not a deliverable. Declare dependencies in pyproject.toml, commit a lock file, and pin the interpreter version, so the customer's build produces the same environment as yours. Tools such as uv or Poetry handle resolution and virtual environments; a container image removes the remaining differences. Read configuration from environment variables and fail at startup with a clear message when one is missing. In restricted networks the public package index may be unreachable, so learn early whether there is an internal mirror and whether wheels must be vendored. Ship a single entry point command and a short runbook.
body.heading: Making it run somewhere else

subtopics.title: Packaging and reproducible environments

concepts.summary: Python is the default language for field integration work because one language covers throwaway scripts, data transformation, HTTP services and the whole AI library ecosystem. The skill is less about syntax than about writing small programs that survive real customer data: typed at the boundaries, concurrent where the work is I/O bound, and packaged so they run the same way inside someone else's environment.
concepts.title: Python for integrations, services and data transformation

concepts.in_practice: Teams that deploy to customers tend to standardize a starter repository: strict TypeScript, one schema library, one HTTP framework, lint and type check in CI, and a pinned Node version. When a new integration starts, the engineer generates or hand-writes types for the customer's API, wraps every response in a schema parse, and writes the business logic against those types. Shared types between the backend and the front end live in one package so a contract change breaks the build instead of production. Scripts that began as one-offs get promoted into a tools directory with real argument parsing once they are run a second time.

body.body: TypeScript checks shapes, not names: any value with the required properties satisfies a type. The everyday building blocks are primitives, arrays, object types, optional properties, union types and literal types. A union says a value is one of several shapes, and narrowing is how the compiler learns which one inside a branch, through typeof checks, the in operator, equality checks or a shared literal field. That last pattern, a discriminated union, is the best way to model API responses and event payloads, because a switch over the discriminant is checked for exhaustiveness. Turn on strict mode, avoid any, and use unknown for data that has not been validated yet.
body.heading: Structural types, unions and narrowing

subtopics.title: Modeling data with the type system

body.body: Types are erased during compilation, so a type annotation on a parsed JSON response is a claim, not a check. If the customer's API returns a string where you declared a number, the program continues with wrong data until something far away breaks. The fix is a schema library such as Zod or Valibot: define the schema once, parse unknown input through it, and infer the static type from the schema so the two can never drift. Apply this at every boundary: HTTP responses, webhook bodies, environment variables, configuration files and model outputs. Inside the boundary, trust the types and keep validation out of business logic.
body.heading: Closing the gap between compile time and the wire

subtopics.title: Runtime validation: types do not exist at runtime

body.body: Node.js runs JavaScript on a single thread and hands I/O to the operating system or a small thread pool, resuming your code through callbacks when results arrive. This lets one process hold thousands of open connections cheaply, and it also means any long synchronous computation blocks every request. Promises and async and await are the standard way to write this code. Promise.all runs operations concurrently and rejects on the first failure, while Promise.allSettled reports every outcome. A forgotten await produces a floating promise whose error is never handled, so enable the lint rule that catches it. CPU-heavy work belongs in worker threads or a separate service.
body.heading: One thread, non-blocking I/O

subtopics.title: The Node.js event loop and async code

body.body: The durable parts of a Node service are the same in any framework: a typed request and response contract, schema validation on input, structured logging with a request id, graceful shutdown on SIGTERM so in-flight requests finish, and health endpoints for the orchestrator. What changes over time is the ecosystem: ES modules versus CommonJS, built-in fetch and test runner in recent Node versions, and alternative runtimes such as Bun and Deno. Pin the runtime version in the repository and in the container image so the customer's environment matches.
body.heading: Beyond the basic server

subtopics.title: HTTP services in Node with TypeScript

body.body: A TypeScript project is defined by package.json for dependencies and scripts, a lock file, and tsconfig.json for compiler options. For scripts and command line tools, run TypeScript directly with a runner such as tsx, or use the type stripping support in recent Node versions, and keep tsc with noEmit as the type check step in CI. ESLint with the TypeScript plugin and Prettier or Biome keep a shared repository consistent. Small internal tools, such as a data backfill command or a configuration validator, are worth writing as proper CLI entry points with argument parsing and exit codes, because they get reused by the customer's team long after the engagement.
body.heading: The minimum viable toolchain

subtopics.title: Tooling, scripts and project setup

concepts.summary: TypeScript adds a static, structural type system on top of JavaScript and compiles away to plain JavaScript that Node.js runs on a single-threaded event loop. In field work it is the language of customer-facing applications, of many SaaS SDKs, and of the tooling around them, so an engineer needs to model external data precisely in types and to understand what the runtime does with asynchronous code.
concepts.title: TypeScript and Node.js for services and tooling

concepts.in_practice: A typical customer application starts from a Next.js template with TypeScript, a component library and an authentication provider already wired in. The engineer builds pages as server components that query Postgres directly, adds client components only for interactive pieces such as a chat panel or an editable table, and streams model output through a route handler. Every pull request produces a preview deployment that is shared with the customer for feedback, and the same build is later promoted to the customer's own cloud as a container when security review requires it.

body.body: The discipline from Thinking in React still decides whether an application stays maintainable: break the interface into a component hierarchy, build a static version first, find the minimal state, and decide which component owns each piece. Most bugs in fast-built customer applications come from duplicated or derived state held in several places. Compute derived values during render, lift shared state to the closest common parent, and reach for effects only to synchronize with systems outside React.
body.heading: The part worth revisiting

subtopics.title: Components, props and state

body.body: In the Next.js App Router, folders under the app directory define URL segments and special files define behavior: page for the route's interface, layout for chrome shared by child routes, loading for a fallback shown while content streams, error for an error boundary, and route for an HTTP endpoint. Dynamic segments are folders in square brackets. Layouts keep their state across navigation between child routes, which makes shells such as a sidebar and a conversation list cheap to build.
body.heading: File-system routing

body.body: Components in the App Router are server components by default. They render on the server, can be async, can read a database or call an internal API directly, and send no component JavaScript to the browser. A file that starts with the use client directive marks a client boundary: it and what it imports are bundled for the browser and can use state, effects and event handlers. The practical rule is to keep data access and secrets in server components and push the client boundary down to the smallest interactive leaf. Props that cross from server to client must be serializable.
body.heading: Where code runs

subtopics.title: The App Router: server and client components

body.body: Reads happen in server components with ordinary async code, so a page can await a query and render the result with no client-side fetching layer. Writes go through server functions, marked with the use server directive and called from forms or event handlers, or through route handlers when an external system needs a plain HTTP endpoint such as a webhook. After a write, revalidate the affected path or tag so cached pages refresh. Treat every server function as a public endpoint: authenticate, authorize and validate its input, because it can be invoked directly.
body.heading: Reading and writing

body.body: Model responses arrive token by token, and users expect to see them that way. Suspense boundaries let the server send the page shell immediately and stream slower sections as they resolve. For chat-style output, a route handler returns a streamed response that a client component reads incrementally and appends to state. Design the interface around the slow path: show tool calls and intermediate steps as they happen, allow cancellation, and persist the conversation on the server so a refresh does not lose work. Caching defaults have changed between major Next.js versions, so check the behavior of the version in use.
body.heading: Streaming for AI interfaces

subtopics.title: Data fetching, mutations and streaming

body.body: Enterprise customers expect single sign-on through their identity provider, usually by OpenID Connect or SAML, so plan for it from the first demo rather than shipping a password form. Keep the session in an HTTP-only cookie, check it on the server for every page and every server function, and enforce data access rules in the data layer, not only by hiding buttons. Secrets and model API keys stay in server-only code and environment variables. Decide the hosting target early: a managed platform is fastest, while many customers require a container in their own cloud account, which Next.js supports through a standalone Node build.
body.heading: What a customer application needs before it is real

subtopics.title: Authentication, authorization and customer deployment concerns

body.body: In field work the preview link is a communication tool as much as an engineering one: each pull request yields a URL that a customer stakeholder can click and react to the same day. Protect previews behind authentication and seed them with scrubbed data. Keep a thin end-to-end suite on the critical flow, such as sign in, submit a request and see a result, and stub the model call so tests are deterministic.
body.heading: The feedback loop with the customer

subtopics.title: Preview deployments and UI testing

concepts.summary: Customers judge an AI deployment by the screen their people use, so a forward deployed engineer is often expected to build that screen as well as the backend. React supplies the component model, and Next.js wraps it in a full-stack framework with routing, server rendering and server-side data access in one codebase, which is why it is the common choice for pilot and production customer applications.
concepts.title: Full-stack customer applications with React and Next.js

concepts.in_practice: On a new engagement the first database task is usually discovery: a read-only role, a pass through the catalog, column profiling, and a mapping document reviewed with the customer's domain expert. For systems the team builds, schemas are managed with a migration tool in the application repository, constraints carry the invariants, and indexes are added after looking at real query plans from slow query logs or pg_stat_statements. Large event or log tables are range partitioned by time from the start so retention is a partition drop. Changes to big production tables are rehearsed on a copy and applied with concurrent index builds and short lock timeouts.

body.body: A schema is the most durable documentation a system has. Model entities as tables with a primary key, express relationships with foreign keys, and encode invariants as NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK constraints so bad data is rejected at write time instead of discovered in a report. Choose types precisely: timestamptz for instants, numeric for money, uuid or bigint identity columns for keys, and jsonb for semi-structured payloads that do not justify columns yet. Normalize by default and denormalize deliberately for read paths you have measured. Schema changes go through versioned migrations, and on large tables you need to know which changes take locks that block writes.
body.heading: Let the database enforce the rules

subtopics.title: Schema design and constraints in Postgres

body.body: An index is a separate ordered structure that lets the database find rows without scanning the table. The default in Postgres is the B-tree, which serves equality and range conditions and can return rows already sorted. In a multicolumn B-tree the column order matters: the index is most useful when the query constrains the leading columns, so put equality columns first and the range or sort column after them. Other index types fit other data: GIN for jsonb containment, arrays and full-text search, GiST for geometric and range types, and BRIN for very large tables whose values correlate with physical order, such as append-only timestamps.
body.heading: How an index helps

body.body: A partial index covers only rows matching a predicate, which keeps it small when queries always filter the same way, for example on unprocessed rows. An expression index stores the result of a function such as lower of an email, and is used only when the query uses the same expression. Covering indexes add non-key columns with INCLUDE so a query can be answered by an index-only scan. Every index slows writes and takes space, so add them in response to real queries. On a busy production table, build with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking writes.
body.heading: Refinements and costs

subtopics.title: Indexing: types, column order and trade-offs

body.body: EXPLAIN shows the plan the planner chose as a tree of nodes, each with an estimated cost and row count. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and adds real timings and row counts, and the BUFFERS option shows how many pages were read. Read from the innermost nodes outward. The key signals are a sequential scan on a large table where few rows are needed, a large gap between estimated and actual rows, which points to stale or missing statistics, and a nested loop executed many thousands of times. Remember that ANALYZE executes the statement, so wrap data-modifying queries in a transaction and roll back.
body.heading: From slow query to cause

subtopics.title: Reading query plans with EXPLAIN

body.body: Postgres can split one logical table into child tables by range, list or hash on a partition key. The planner uses partition pruning to skip children that cannot match the query's conditions, so queries must filter on the key to benefit. The larger operational win is data lifecycle: dropping or detaching a month-old partition is a fast metadata change, while deleting the same rows is slow and leaves bloat. The constraints are real: a primary key or unique constraint must include the partition key columns, too many partitions increases planning time, and a poor key choice gives no pruning at all. Partition when a table is large and access is naturally bounded by time or tenant.
body.heading: Declarative partitioning and when it pays off

subtopics.title: Table partitioning

body.body: Start with the catalog: information_schema and the pg_catalog tables list every table, column, type, constraint and index, and table statistics show which tables are large and actively written. Declared foreign keys give the reliable relationships; for the rest, infer candidates from column names and confirm by checking that values in one column actually exist in the other. Profile each important column for null rate, distinct count and value distribution, since a status column with eleven values tells you more than its name. Then sit with someone who uses the system, trace one real business record across tables, and write down the mapping as a glossary the customer signs off on.
body.heading: A repeatable discovery method

body.body: Ask for a read-only role scoped to the schemas you need, and prefer a replica or a snapshot over the primary. Set a statement timeout for your session so an accidental cross join cannot run for an hour. Sample with LIMIT while exploring, and check the plan before running anything over a large table. Record every assumption about meaning, such as which timestamp is the business date and how soft deletes are flagged, because those assumptions are where integrations and AI features silently go wrong.
body.heading: Working safely on someone else's database

subtopics.title: Mapping an undocumented customer schema to business concepts

concepts.summary: Almost every deployment ends up reading from or writing to a relational database, and Postgres is the one most often named. The work has two halves: designing schemas, indexes and partitions for the systems you build, and reading a customer's existing, often undocumented, schema well enough to map it to business concepts and query it without hurting production.
concepts.title: SQL and data systems: schemas, indexing and partitioning in Postgres

concepts.in_practice: A team using these tools well commits an instruction file and a small set of shared commands to each repository, so every session starts with the same build, test and convention knowledge. Engineers begin non-trivial changes in a read-only planning step, approve the plan, and let the agent implement against a test it can run. Pull requests stay small and are reviewed by a human who reads the full diff, with CI as the arbiter of whether anything passes. On customer engagements the tool, account type and permitted data are agreed in writing before the first session, and agents run with the minimum permissions and no production credentials.

body.body: An agent that starts editing immediately will solve the problem it guessed at. The reliable loop is to have it read the relevant code first and explain how the area works, then produce a plan you review before any file changes, then implement in small steps, then prove the result by running tests, a type check or the application itself. Tools support this directly, for example a plan mode that restricts the agent to read-only actions until the plan is approved. The same loop is the fastest way into an unfamiliar customer codebase: ask where a request enters, how data flows and which tests cover it before changing anything.
body.heading: Why the order matters

body.body: The largest quality lever is a verification signal the agent can run on its own: a failing test that should pass, an expected output, a screenshot to match, or a lint and type check command. Without one, the agent stops when the code looks plausible. State the task with the target behavior, the files or patterns to follow, and the command that proves success. Keep tasks scoped to one reviewable change, and start a fresh session when the context fills with unrelated history, since stale context degrades results.
body.heading: Giving the agent a way to check itself

subtopics.title: The core workflow: explore, plan, implement, verify

body.body: Each tool reads a persistent instruction file at the start of a session: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, rules files for Cursor, and AGENTS.md for Codex. Put there what the agent cannot infer from the code: the build and test commands, branch and commit conventions, directories that must not be touched, and the non-obvious architectural rules. Keep it short and specific, because long instruction files get diluted. Repeated workflows, such as opening a pull request or running a migration check, belong in reusable commands or skills so every engineer on the engagement invokes the same procedure. Connections to external systems such as issue trackers or databases are added through Model Context Protocol servers.
body.heading: Teaching the tool the repository

subtopics.title: Project context: instruction files, rules and reusable commands

body.body: Beyond ordinary review, watch for the mistakes agents make more often than people do: tests weakened or deleted to get a green run, errors swallowed by broad exception handlers, invented library functions or configuration options, duplicated helpers where one already exists, and changes that drift outside the requested scope. Read the diff, not the agent's summary of the diff, and treat a claim that tests pass as unverified until CI shows it.
body.heading: Failure modes specific to generated code

subtopics.title: Reviewing and testing generated code

body.body: Coding agents run shell commands with your credentials, so the permission model matters. Tools provide modes that range from asking before every edit or command to allowing a defined set automatically, plus allow and deny lists for specific commands and paths. Hooks run your own scripts before or after tool calls and can block an action deterministically, which is stronger than an instruction the model may ignore. Run unattended or broadly permitted sessions inside a sandbox or container without production credentials. Treat content the agent reads from the web, issues or documents as untrusted, because it can carry injected instructions.
body.heading: Controlling what the agent can do

body.body: Before using any AI tool on a customer's code, confirm that their policy and your contract allow it, which provider and data retention terms apply, and whether the code may leave their network at all. Some customers require a specific approved tool, an enterprise account, or a cloud-hosted model endpoint inside their own tenancy. Keep secrets and personal data out of prompts and out of files the agent reads. Follow the customer's review process exactly, and disclose AI assistance where their contribution rules ask for it.
body.heading: Customer-specific obligations

subtopics.title: Permissions, safety and working in customer repositories

body.body: The remaining points are mechanical. Isolate parallel sessions with git worktrees so agents do not overwrite each other. Use subagents to keep exploration out of the main context window. Run the tool non-interactively in CI for narrow jobs such as triaging a failing build or drafting a review, with a tightly restricted tool list. Parallelism multiplies review load, so cap it at what one person can actually read.
body.heading: Scaling beyond one session

subtopics.title: Parallel sessions, subagents and headless automation

concepts.summary: Agentic coding tools read a repository, run commands, edit files and iterate on test results, which changes the engineer's job from typing code to directing and verifying it. For a forward deployed engineer the gain is speed in unfamiliar customer codebases, and the obligation is unchanged: the person who merges the change owns its correctness, security and fit with the customer's standards.
concepts.title: Shipping production code with Claude Code and other AI coding tools

This module covers the five foundations that work rests on: Python, TypeScript on Node.js, React with Next.js, Postgres, and AI coding tools used with production discipline.

import os, requests

def get_token():
    r = requests.post(os.environ["TOKEN_URL"], data={
        "grant_type": "client_credentials",
        "scope": "contacts.read",
    }, auth=(os.environ["CLIENT_ID"], os.environ["CLIENT_SECRET"]), timeout=10)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["access_token"]

def list_contacts(token):
    url, out = os.environ["API_BASE"] + "/contacts", []
    while url:
        r = requests.get(url, headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}, timeout=10)
        r.raise_for_status()
        body = r.json()
        out += body["items"]
        url = body.get("next")  # cursor link, absent on last page
    return out

They generate or hand-write a thin typed client, put schema validation and structured logging at the boundary, and wrap it with one shared policy for timeouts, retries, backoff and token refresh. Read sync ships first with a watermark and a reconciliation count against the source; writeback ships second, behind an upsert key and a dry-run mode that logs intended changes, and is enabled for a handful of records before it is opened to the whole tenant.

JSON Schema: Creating your first schema

body.body: HTTP is a stateless client-server protocol: every request carries a method, a path, headers and an optional body, and every response carries a status code. As a consumer, the method semantics decide your retry policy. GET, PUT and DELETE are defined as idempotent, so a timed-out call can be repeated; POST is not, so a blind retry can create a second record. Status classes decide the next action: 4xx means fix the request or the credentials, 429 means slow down, 5xx means retry later. Vendor APIs often bend these rules, so confirm actual behavior in a sandbox before trusting the documentation.
body.heading: What matters when you consume instead of serve

subtopics.title: HTTP semantics from the consumer side

body.body: JSON has six value kinds: object, array, string, number, true or false, and null. The format does not define integer width, dates, or what to do with duplicate keys, and that is where integrations break. Large identifiers lose precision when a parser reads them as floating point, so many APIs send them as strings. Timestamps arrive as strings in whatever format the vendor chose. Missing key, null and empty string are three different things that source systems use inconsistently. Decide explicitly how each maps into your own model instead of letting the parser decide.
body.heading: JSON and its sharp edges

body.body: JSON Schema describes the shape of a document: types, required properties, enums, formats and nested structures. Validating every inbound payload against a schema at the boundary turns silent data corruption into a loud, attributable error. OpenAPI wraps the same idea around a whole HTTP API: paths, operations, parameters, request and response schemas, and security schemes such as OAuth 2.0 flows and scopes. When a vendor publishes an OpenAPI document, generate a typed client from it and diff new versions in CI. When they do not, write the schema yourself from observed traffic and treat it as your contract test.
body.heading: Schemas at the boundary

subtopics.title: JSON, JSON Schema and OpenAPI as the contract

body.body: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that lets an application obtain limited access to an HTTP service without holding the user's password. It defines four roles. The resource owner is the user or organization that owns the data. The client is your application. The authorization server authenticates the owner, collects consent and issues tokens. The resource server is the API that accepts those tokens. In enterprise SaaS the authorization server and resource server are usually the same vendor, and the customer's admin, not the end user, often has to approve your client before anyone can connect.
body.heading: The four roles

body.body: The authorization code grant is for acting on behalf of a user: the browser is redirected to the authorization server, the user consents, and your backend exchanges the returned code for tokens. Add PKCE and a state parameter to protect the exchange. The client credentials grant is for machine to machine access where the client acts as itself, which is typical for backend sync jobs and service accounts. The original specification also defines the implicit and resource owner password grants; current guidance treats both as legacy and they should not be used for new work. A refresh token lets the client obtain new access tokens without user interaction.
body.heading: Choosing a grant

subtopics.title: OAuth 2.0 roles and grant types

body.body: Access tokens are short lived by design, so the client must handle expiry as a normal path. Cache the token with its expiry time, refresh slightly early, and on a 401 refresh once and retry once. Some authorization servers rotate the refresh token on every use, so concurrent workers must serialize the refresh or one of them will be logged out. Request the narrowest scopes that the workflow needs; security reviewers will ask why each one is there. In a multi-tenant deployment, store tokens per customer tenant, encrypted, in a secrets manager or an encrypted column, never in logs, prompts or agent context.
body.heading: Running tokens in production

body.body: When an LLM agent calls APIs through tools, the token defines the blast radius of a bad decision. Keep the token inside the tool implementation so the model never sees it. Prefer per-user delegated tokens over one powerful service account, so the agent can only do what the requesting user could do, and the vendor's audit log shows who acted. Split read scopes from write scopes and gate write tools behind approval where the action is hard to undo.
body.heading: What an AI agent changes

subtopics.title: Token lifecycle, scopes and secret storage

body.body: Bulk reads go through pagination. Cursor based pagination returns an opaque pointer to the next page and stays stable while data changes; offset pagination can skip or repeat rows when records are inserted mid-scan. For incremental sync, filter on a last-modified field and keep a watermark, overlapping slightly and deduplicating by id. Respect rate limits: read the limit headers the vendor returns, honor Retry-After on 429, and back off exponentially with jitter. Budget the limit across all your workers for a tenant, since the quota is usually shared with the customer's other integrations.
body.heading: Reading at volume

body.body: Writeback to a CRM or ERP is where mistakes become visible to the customer. A timeout does not tell you whether the write happened. Use an idempotency key header where the API supports it, or an upsert on an external id field that you control, so repeating the call is harmless. Otherwise read before write. Record every outbound mutation with request id, tenant, payload hash and response, so a wrong update can be traced and reversed.
body.heading: Writing without duplicates

subtopics.title: Resilient clients: pagination, rate limits and safe writeback

concepts.summary: Most enterprise integrations are HTTP calls carrying JSON, authorized by an OAuth 2.0 access token. The job of a forward deployed engineer is less about designing a clean API and more about consuming someone else's imperfect one safely: getting delegated access approved, validating payloads, surviving rate limits and writing back to a system of record without creating duplicates. This lesson moves from the protocol layer, through data contracts, to authorization and resilient client design.
concepts.title: REST APIs, JSON and OAuth 2.0 authentication

import hmac, hashlib, os
from flask import Flask, request, abort

app = Flask(__name__)
SECRET = os.environ["WEBHOOK_SECRET"].encode()

@app.post("/webhooks/crm")
def receive():
    raw = request.get_data()  # verify the raw bytes, not parsed JSON
    want = "sha256=" + hmac.new(SECRET, raw, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    got = request.headers.get("X-Signature-256", "")
    if not hmac.compare_digest(got, want):
        abort(401)
    event = request.get_json()
    enqueue(key=event["object_id"], event_id=event["id"], payload=raw)
    return "", 204  # ack fast; consumers dedupe on event_id

On customer-owned Kafka, topic creation, ACLs and schema registration go through the customer's platform team, so those requests are filed in the first week of the engagement rather than the last.

sources.title: Stripe Docs: Receive events in your webhook endpoint

body.body: A webhook is an HTTP POST that a provider sends to an endpoint you register when a subscribed event occurs. The endpoint is public, so authenticity comes from a signature: the provider computes an HMAC over the raw request body with a shared secret and sends it in a header, and you recompute it and compare in constant time. Verify against the raw bytes, before any JSON parsing or re-serialization. Many providers also sign a timestamp so you can reject old requests and limit replay. Rotate the secret like any other credential.
body.heading: The receiver contract

body.body: Providers expect a 2xx response within a short timeout and treat anything else as a failed delivery. The receiver should therefore do three things only: verify the signature, persist or enqueue the event, and return success. Calling an LLM, a CRM or a database migration inside the request handler leads to timeouts, provider retries and duplicated work. Subscribe only to the event types you need, and keep the provider's delivery log and redelivery tools in your runbook, since they are the first place to look when events go missing.
body.heading: Acknowledge fast, work later

subtopics.title: Receiving webhooks: verify, acknowledge, defer

body.body: Webhook delivery is at-least-once and unordered in practice. Providers retry on failure, so the same event can arrive more than once, and an update can arrive before the create it follows. Deduplicate on the provider's event id with a unique constraint or a processed-events table, written in the same transaction as the side effect. For ordering, do not trust arrival order: compare a version or timestamp on the object, or treat the event as a hint and fetch current state from the API before acting.
body.heading: Design for at-least-once

body.body: Events can be lost entirely, for example during an outage longer than the provider's retry window or after an endpoint is auto-disabled. Pair every webhook subscription with a periodic reconciliation job that lists recently modified objects through the API and repairs differences. The webhook gives low latency; the reconciliation gives correctness.
body.heading: Closing the gaps

subtopics.title: Duplicates, ordering and reconciliation

body.body: Kafka stores events durably in topics. An event has a key, a value, a timestamp and optional headers. Each topic is split into partitions, which are append-only logs spread across brokers and replicated for fault tolerance. Events with the same key go to the same partition, and order is guaranteed only within a partition, so the key choice is the ordering decision: key by customer or entity id when per-entity order matters. Unlike a traditional queue, reading does not delete; events are retained for a configured time or size, so consumers can replay.
body.heading: A distributed commit log

body.body: Consumers track their position as an offset per partition. Consumers that share a group id divide the partitions among themselves, which gives parallelism up to the partition count; separate groups each receive the full stream independently, which is how one topic feeds a CRM writeback service and an AI agent trigger at the same time. Consumer lag, the distance between the latest offset and the committed offset, is the primary health signal. Rebalances occur when members join or leave and briefly pause consumption.
body.heading: Consumers and scaling

subtopics.title: Kafka's model: topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups

body.body: Commit the offset after processing and you get at-least-once: a crash between the side effect and the commit means reprocessing. Commit before and you get at-most-once. Kafka's idempotent producer removes duplicates caused by producer retries, and transactions make a consume-transform-produce cycle atomic within Kafka. Neither extends to an external HTTP call or database write, so consumers that touch other systems still need idempotent handlers. When a service must update its database and publish an event together, write the event to an outbox table in the same transaction and relay it to Kafka.
body.heading: What exactly-once really covers

body.body: A topic is a shared API. Define event schemas in Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema, register them, and enforce compatibility rules so a producer cannot break existing consumers. A record that always fails must not block its partition: retry a bounded number of times, then route it to a dead letter topic with the error and original offset, alert, and provide a replay path once the bug is fixed.
body.heading: Contracts and bad records

subtopics.title: Delivery guarantees, schemas and poison messages

body.body: A common deployment shape is a thin webhook ingress service that verifies each provider's signature, wraps the payload in a standard envelope with source, event id, tenant and received time, and produces it to Kafka keyed by entity id. Everything downstream consumes from the log, so a slow or failing consumer never causes provider retries, and a new use case is a new consumer group replaying history. In restricted environments the cluster is rarely yours: expect TLS and SASL authentication, per-topic ACLs requested through a platform team, and network rules that decide where the ingress can run. Alternatives such as RabbitMQ or NATS appear where a customer needs routing or lightweight messaging more than a replayable log.
body.heading: The ingress pattern

subtopics.title: Bridging webhooks into the customer's event backbone

concepts.summary: Polling an API tells you what changed eventually; events tell you when it changes. Webhooks are the push mechanism SaaS vendors expose over plain HTTP, and Kafka is the durable, replayable log enterprises use to move events between their own systems. This lesson covers how to receive webhooks safely, how Kafka's model works, what delivery guarantees you actually get, and how the two are combined in a customer deployment.
concepts.title: Webhooks and event-driven integrations with Kafka

  F -->|remaining capabilities| L[Legacy system]

concepts.in_practice: A team begins with discovery: an inventory of every consumer, integration and scheduled job touching the legacy system, plus samples of real data. They put a routing facade or adapter in front, build the anti-corruption layer with tests drawn from those samples, and move one narrow capability first to prove routing, sync and rollback. Schema changes follow expand, migrate, contract as numbered migration scripts. Data moves by backfill plus change data capture, with reconciliation reports reviewed with business owners, a period of parallel running, and a rehearsed cutover runbook. The engagement tracks a decommission date as a deliverable, because customers judge the migration by the day the old tool is switched off.

body.body: A big-bang rewrite delivers no value until the end and concentrates all risk in one cutover. The strangler fig pattern grows the new system around the old one instead. A facade or proxy sits in front of the legacy system and intercepts requests. One capability at a time is implemented in the new system, and the facade routes that slice of traffic to it while everything else still goes to legacy. Over time the legacy system handles less and less until it can be retired, and then the facade itself can be removed.
body.heading: The pattern

body.body: Choose seams by business capability and by where interception is possible: an HTTP route, a message type, a batch job, a UI screen. Start with a slice that is low risk but real, so the routing and rollback machinery is proven early. Route by percentage or by tenant, and keep the ability to send traffic back. The hard part is shared data: while both systems are live, decide which one owns each entity and synchronize the other. The pattern is poor value for small systems or where requests cannot be intercepted.
body.heading: Making it work

subtopics.title: Strangler fig: replace incrementally behind a facade

body.body: Legacy systems carry their own semantics: overloaded status codes, fixed-width fields, composite keys, flags whose meaning depends on the year the record was created. If the new system calls them directly, those concepts leak into its domain model and prompts. An anti-corruption layer is a facade or adapter between the two that translates in both directions, so the new system speaks only its own model and the legacy system is unchanged. It can live as a module inside the new service or as a separate service when several consumers need it.
body.heading: Translation at the boundary

body.body: The layer adds a network hop, latency and something else to operate and scale, so keep it thin: mapping, validation and protocol conversion, no business logic. Give it its own contract tests built from real legacy samples, including the ugly ones. For AI workloads it is also the right place to normalize codes into readable labels before data reaches a model. Decide up front whether it is temporary, retired with the legacy system, or permanent because the legacy system is staying.
body.heading: Costs and lifecycle

subtopics.title: Anti-corruption layer: keep the legacy model out

body.body: Many systems of record predate REST. In rough order of preference: a documented service interface such as SOAP or a vendor SDK; an existing message queue or scheduled file export over SFTP in CSV, fixed-width or XML; read access to a database replica or reporting views; change data capture from the database transaction log, which streams inserts, updates and deletes without touching application code; and finally UI automation or screen scraping when nothing else exists. Each step down the list is more brittle and less supported by the vendor.
body.heading: Options, from best to worst

body.body: Ask who owns the system and whether direct database access voids support. Find the batch windows, since many legacy systems are only consistent after a nightly job. Measure how much extra load the system tolerates before querying it in a loop. Prefer reading from a replica and writing through the supported interface, because writing straight to legacy tables bypasses validation that lives in application code. Capture real samples early: encodings, date formats and sentinel values such as all nines are where the schedule slips.
body.heading: Constraints to check early

subtopics.title: Finding an integration surface when there is no API

body.body: Parallel change makes a breaking interface change safe by splitting it into three phases. Expand: add the new form alongside the old, for example a new column, field or endpoint, so both are valid. Migrate: move every producer and consumer to the new form and backfill existing data, usually with dual writes during the transition. Contract: remove the old form once nothing uses it. Each phase is deployed separately and is reversible until contract, which is what allows zero-downtime change while old and new code run side by side.
body.heading: Expand, migrate, contract

body.body: Evolutionary database design treats every schema change as a small, ordered migration script kept in version control and applied automatically through every environment, with data migration included in the same script as the structural change. In a legacy migration this gives a repeatable path from the old shape to the new one that can be rehearsed against production copies. Backfill in batches to avoid long locks, and verify that no reader still depends on the old form before you contract, using query logs or access metrics.
body.heading: Schema as versioned code

subtopics.title: Parallel change and evolutionary database design

body.body: Beyond automated reconciliation and backfills, the cutover itself needs a plan. Run the new system in shadow or parallel so its outputs are compared with legacy on live traffic before it becomes authoritative. Define explicit go or no-go criteria, a freeze window, the order of switching writers before readers, and a rollback path with a deadline after which rolling back means data loss. After cutover, keep legacy read-only for an agreed period, then archive data to meet retention rules, revoke credentials, remove integrations and stop paying for it. A migration is finished when the old system is off, not when the new one is on.
body.heading: The last mile

subtopics.title: Validated cutover and decommissioning

concepts.summary: Customers buy AI systems to change how work is done, but the work still runs through systems that are old, poorly documented and business critical. The skill is to integrate with them through whatever interface exists, shield the new system from their data model, and move functionality and data across in small reversible steps until the old tool can be switched off. This lesson covers the core patterns: strangler fig, anti-corruption layer, parallel change, and a validated cutover.
concepts.title: Integrating legacy systems and running migrations

modules.intro: Forward deployed work lives or dies on connecting an AI system to the customer's real systems of record: CRMs, ERPs, ticketing tools, event buses and decades-old databases. This module covers the request/response contract (HTTP, JSON, OAuth 2.0), the push and streaming contract (webhooks and Kafka), and the patterns for integrating with and migrating off legacy systems without breaking the business.
modules.title: APIs and Enterprise Integrations

client = anthropic.Anthropic()  # reads the API key from the environment
