sequenceDiagram
  participant App
  participant API as Model API
  participant Tok as Tokenizer
  participant M as Model
  App->>API: system, messages, max_tokens, params
  API->>Tok: text
  Tok->>M: token ids within context window
  loop one token per step
    M-->>API: next token
  end
  API-->>App: streamed deltas, stop reason, usage

concepts.in_practice: On a customer engagement the team first builds a token and cost model for the target workflow: typical input size, expected output size, calls per transaction and transactions per day, per model tier. They wrap the provider SDK in a thin client that sets timeouts and retries with backoff on rate limit and overload errors, records model id, token usage, stop reason and latency for every call, and enforces a maximum output size. Model ids are pinned in configuration instead of floating aliases so behavior does not shift under a release. Streaming is turned on for anything a person waits on, caching is applied to the stable prefix, and a cheaper model is tried on each step with the evaluation set deciding whether quality holds.

body.body: Models do not read characters or words. A tokenizer splits text into subword units from a fixed vocabulary and maps each to an integer id; the model only ever sees those ids. Common English words are often a single token, while rare words, identifiers, non-English text and numbers split into several. A rough planning figure for English prose is three to four characters per token, but JSON, code and tables are noticeably denser in tokens than their character count suggests.
body.heading: What a token is

body.body: Tokens are the unit for everything a provider meters: the context limit, the output limit, rate limits and price. Token counts differ between model families because each uses its own tokenizer, so a prompt that fits one model may not fit another. Measure with the provider's token counting endpoint or library rather than estimating, and log input and output token counts from every response so that cost and capacity questions can be answered from data.
body.heading: Why it matters in an application

subtopics.title: Tokens and tokenization

body.body: The Transformer replaced recurrence with attention. Each token id becomes an embedding vector, positional information is added, and a stack of layers repeatedly applies self-attention followed by a feed-forward network. In self-attention every position computes query, key and value vectors and takes a weighted mix of the other positions, so any token can directly use information from any other token in the window. Multiple attention heads run in parallel and learn different relationships. The final layer produces a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token.
body.heading: The architecture in one pass

body.body: Generation is autoregressive: the model samples one token, appends it, and runs again. Output is therefore produced sequentially and output tokens dominate latency, while input is processed in parallel. The model has no memory outside the window and no notion of truth, only of likely continuations, which is why fluent but wrong answers occur when the needed facts are absent. Sampling settings such as temperature change how the distribution is drawn from, so identical requests can return different text.
body.heading: Consequences for builders

subtopics.title: Transformers and next-token prediction

body.body: The context window is the total number of tokens the model can consider in one request: system prompt, tool definitions, the full conversation history, retrieved documents, tool results, and the output being generated. Reasoning or thinking tokens, where a model supports them, also consume budget. Because the API is stateless, each turn resends the whole history, so input size grows linearly with turns and total tokens billed across a conversation grow roughly quadratically unless history is trimmed or cached.
body.heading: What counts against the window

body.body: Treat the window as working memory with a hard ceiling and a soft quality limit. Exceeding the ceiling yields an error or truncation depending on provider and model; well before that, very long contexts can dilute attention to the important parts. Standard techniques are to reserve space for the output, summarize or drop old turns, keep tool results compact, retrieve only what the current step needs, and place long reference material before the question that uses it.
body.heading: Managing it

subtopics.title: The context window as a budget

body.body: Provider APIs converge on the same shape: a model id, a system or developer instruction, an ordered list of messages with roles such as user and assistant, optional tool definitions, and generation settings. The key settings are a maximum output token count, temperature or other sampling controls, and stop sequences. The response carries content blocks, a stop reason (finished naturally, hit the output limit, or requested a tool) and a usage object with token counts. Always branch on the stop reason: a response cut off by the output limit is a different outcome from a completed answer and should not be parsed as one.
body.heading: Shape of a request and response

subtopics.title: Model API requests and parameters

body.body: Cost is input tokens times input price plus output tokens times output price, with output usually priced several times higher. Latency splits into time to first token, driven by input size and queueing, and generation time, driven by output length. Streaming returns tokens as they are produced, which improves perceived latency and lets a client cancel early. Prompt caching lets a stable prefix such as the system prompt, tool definitions and reference documents be reused across requests at a reduced rate, so order content from most stable to most variable. Batch endpoints trade latency for a lower price on offline work, and smaller models handle routing and extraction steps cheaply.
body.heading: The levers

subtopics.title: Cost, latency, streaming and caching

concepts.summary: A large language model is a function that takes a sequence of tokens and predicts the next one, repeated until a stop condition. Everything an application does with a model, including chat, tools and retrieval, is expressed by what is placed in a bounded context window and sent through a stateless API. Understanding tokens, the window and the request parameters explains most of the cost, latency and failure behavior seen in the field.
concepts.title: How LLMs work inside applications: tokens, context windows and model APIs

code.code:
SYSTEM = """You are a support analyst for a billing platform.
Answer only from the material inside <documents>.
If the answer is not there, reply exactly: NOT_FOUND.
Give the answer inside <answer> tags, one short paragraph."""

def build_user_turn(docs: list[str], question: str) -> str:
    blocks = "\n".join(
        f"<document index=\"{i}\">\n{d}\n</document>" for i, d in enumerate(docs)
    )
    # long reference material first, the question last
    return f"<documents>\n{blocks}\n</documents>\n\nQuestion: {question}"

flowchart TD
  A[Success criteria and real cases] --> B[Prompt template]
  C[Stable context: role, rules, tools] --> D[Assemble window]
  E[Selected documents and history summary] --> D
  F[Current user request] --> D
  B --> D
  D --> G[Model call]
  G --> H[Score against cases]
  H -->|failures by class| B
  H -->|pass| I[Release with pinned model id]

concepts.in_practice: A deployed team starts by writing down success criteria with the customer and collecting a few dozen real inputs, including the awkward ones. The first prompt is plain and explicit; it is run against the cases, failures are read one by one, and each revision targets a named failure class. Prompts live in the repository as templates with typed variables, are reviewed like code, and are tagged with the model id they were tuned for. Customer documents, user input and tool results are wrapped in delimiters and treated as data, never spliced into the instruction text. When context grows, the team measures which sections the answers depend on and removes or summarizes the rest before reaching for a larger window.

body.body: A dependable prompt separates concerns. The system or developer message carries the role, the task, the audience, constraints and the definition of done. Reference material goes in clearly delimited sections, commonly with XML-style tags or headed blocks, so the model can tell instructions from data. The user turn carries the specific request. An output specification states the format and what to do when the answer is unknown. Variable parts are filled from a template so the fixed text stays identical across calls and can be versioned and cached.
body.heading: Parts and their jobs

body.body: Be explicit and direct, as if briefing a capable colleague with no background on the account. State what to do instead of only what to avoid, and give the reason behind a rule, since models generalize better from intent than from a bare prohibition. Put long documents near the top and the question after them. Remove contradictory or leftover instructions; most erratic behavior traces back to a prompt that asks for two incompatible things.
body.heading: Writing instructions that hold

subtopics.title: Anatomy of a production prompt

body.body: Zero-shot prompting gives only instructions; few-shot prompting adds worked input and output pairs. Examples are the strongest signal for format, tone and edge-case handling, and the model will imitate them closely, so make them varied and representative. A set of three to five diverse examples usually outperforms one, and near-identical examples cause the model to copy surface details. Include at least one example of the hard or negative case, such as the correct response when the input lacks the needed information.
body.heading: Few-shot examples

body.body: Asking the model to reason step by step before answering, known as chain of thought, improves accuracy on multi-step problems at the cost of more output tokens; models with a built-in reasoning mode expose this as a setting. Keep the reasoning separate from the final answer so code can parse only the answer. When one prompt tries to do too much, split it into a chain of smaller calls, each with a single job and its own check, which makes failures easy to locate.
body.heading: Reasoning and decomposition

subtopics.title: Examples, reasoning and chaining

body.body: The model can only use what is in the window, and everything in the window competes for attention. Context engineering treats each call as an assembly step: choose the minimal set of facts, documents, history and tool results that the current step requires; compress the rest into summaries or references that can be fetched on demand; and order the result so stable content comes first and the live question last. For long-running work, keep durable state outside the window in files or a database and load slices of it, instead of carrying an ever-growing transcript.
body.heading: Selection, compression and ordering

subtopics.title: Context engineering: selecting and assembling what the model sees

body.body: Prompts are code and should be handled as such: stored in version control, changed through review, and gated by a regression run on a fixed case set before release. Two additions make the loop sturdier. First, re-run the full set whenever the model id changes, since a prompt tuned for one model version can regress on the next. Second, keep failures found in production as new cases, so the set tracks the real input distribution instead of the one imagined at design time.
body.heading: Beyond the basic loop

subtopics.title: Iterating on prompts with evaluations

concepts.summary: Prompt engineering is the practice of writing instructions a model can follow reliably; context engineering is deciding what information occupies the window at each step and in what form. Together they are the main control surface for model behavior that does not require training. The discipline is empirical: define success, write a first version, measure, and change one thing at a time.
concepts.title: Prompt engineering and context engineering

sequenceDiagram
  participant U as User
  participant A as Application
  participant M as Model
  participant S as Customer system
  U->>A: request
  A->>M: messages plus tool definitions
  M-->>A: stop reason tool use, call id, name, arguments
  A->>A: validate arguments, check permissions
  A->>S: execute with timeout and idempotency key
  S-->>A: result or error
  A->>M: tool result tied to call id
  M-->>A: final answer or next tool call
  A-->>U: response

concepts.in_practice: Teams define each output and tool input once as a typed model in application code and generate the JSON Schema from it, so the contract, the validator and the documentation cannot drift. Extraction and classification steps use strict structured outputs; anything touching customer systems goes through tools with narrow scopes, read tools separated from write tools, and writes gated by approval or policy. The executor layer handles timeouts, retries, idempotency keys and logging, and returns errors to the model as tool results. Before go-live the team runs an evaluation set that checks not only final answers but also which tools were called with which arguments, since a correct answer reached through a wrong call is a latent incident.

body.body: Both structured outputs and tool parameters are described with JSON Schema. The working vocabulary is small: type, properties, required, enum for closed sets, items for arrays, nested objects, anyOf for alternatives, and additionalProperties set to false to forbid unexpected keys. Descriptions on fields are read by the model and act as inline instructions. Strict modes accept only a subset of the specification; constraints such as string patterns, numeric ranges or deep recursion may be unsupported or limited depending on the provider, so check the supported subset and enforce the remaining rules in application code after parsing.
body.heading: The parts that matter for models

subtopics.title: JSON Schema as the contract language

body.body: Validation catches shape errors, not meaning errors: a schema-valid object can still hold a wrong value. Add semantic checks after parsing, such as cross-field consistency, ids that must exist in a system of record, and figures that must appear in the source. When a retry is needed, send the validation error text back to the model instead of repeating the same request, and cap attempts so a persistent failure becomes a handled error. Design schemas with an explicit way to express absence, for example a nullable field or a status enum, so the model is not forced to invent a value.
body.heading: Beyond the basic pattern

subtopics.title: Typed outputs with validation and bounded retry

body.body: There are three levels of structure. Asking for JSON in the prompt is best effort. JSON mode guarantees syntactically valid JSON but not a particular shape. Strict structured outputs go further: the provider compiles the schema into a grammar and, at each generation step, masks out tokens that would violate it, so the result always parses and matches the schema. This requires a supported schema subset, typically with every property listed as required and additionalProperties false, with optional values modeled as a union with null.
body.heading: How schema adherence is guaranteed

body.body: A guarantee on shape does not cover every outcome. Output cut off by the token limit can be incomplete, and a model may return a refusal instead of the object, which the API reports separately; handle both before using the data. The first request with a new schema can be slower while the grammar is prepared. Field order in the schema affects quality, since generation is sequential: place a reasoning or evidence field before the verdict field that depends on it.
body.heading: Limits to plan for

subtopics.title: Strict mode and constrained decoding

body.body: The application sends tool definitions, each with a name, a description and an input schema. When the model decides a tool is needed, the response stops with a tool-use stop reason and contains one or more call blocks, each with an id, the tool name and JSON arguments. The application, not the model, executes the call, then sends a new request that includes the earlier assistant turn plus a tool result tied to the call id. The model reads the result and either calls another tool or answers. A model may request several calls in one turn, which can be executed in parallel.
body.heading: Protocol

body.body: A tool choice setting lets the application allow any tool, force a specific tool, or disable tools for a turn; forcing a single tool is a common way to get structured output. Client tools run in application code, while some providers also offer server tools they execute themselves. Cap the number of loop iterations, apply a timeout to every execution, and return failures as tool results marked as errors so the model can recover instead of the loop crashing.
body.heading: Controls

subtopics.title: The tool calling loop

body.body: The description is the main factor in whether a tool is chosen and called correctly. State what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means with its format, and what comes back. Prefer a small number of task-shaped tools over a one-to-one mirror of an internal API, use enums and required fields to shrink the space of bad calls, and give tools distinct names so they are not confused. Keep results compact and relevant, since they are added to the window, and make error messages actionable, for example naming the invalid parameter and the accepted values.
body.heading: Interface design for a model reader

subtopics.title: Designing tools a model can use well

body.body: Arguments produced by a model are untrusted input: validate them against the schema and against the caller's own permissions, since the model must never hold more authority than the user it acts for. Because a loop can retry or repeat a call, give every mutating tool an idempotency key so a duplicate request has no second effect. When calls run in parallel, make sure writes that depend on each other are sequenced by the application. Record each call, its arguments and its result with the request trace so any action can be audited later.
body.heading: Beyond read and write separation

subtopics.title: Side effects, idempotency and approval

concepts.summary: Structured outputs make a model return data that conforms to a schema, so downstream code can consume it without parsing free text. Tool calling extends the same idea to actions: the model emits a typed request to call a function, the application executes it and returns the result, and the model continues. These two mechanisms are what connect a language model to real systems.
concepts.title: Structured outputs and tool calling

concepts.in_practice: A team begins with the customer's real documents and a list of real questions, then labels which passages answer each one; that labeled set drives every later decision. Ingestion runs as a repeatable pipeline keyed on content hashes so changed documents are re-chunked and re-embedded while unchanged ones are skipped, and deletions propagate to the index. The embedding model and its version are stored with every vector, since changing the model means re-embedding the corpus. Online, the service applies tenant and access filters, runs hybrid search, reranks, and assembles a cited context block. Recall at k, latency per stage and the rate of declined answers are tracked on dashboards, and index parameters are tuned against the labeled set instead of by intuition.

sources.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
pgvector: vector similarity search for Postgres

body.body: The original RAG work described a model with two memories: parametric memory in the weights and non-parametric memory in a dense index of passages, queried by a retriever and consumed by a generator. That framing still guides design choices. Knowledge that changes, is private, or must be attributable belongs in the index, where it can be updated or deleted without retraining. When a corpus is small enough to fit in the window, placing it there directly, with prompt caching, can be simpler and more accurate than retrieval, so check corpus size before building a pipeline.
body.heading: The framing behind the pattern

subtopics.title: RAG architecture: parametric and non-parametric memory

body.body: Splitting a document strips each chunk of its surroundings: a passage stating that revenue grew three percent no longer says which company or quarter. Contextual retrieval addresses this by having a model write a short chunk-specific note that situates the passage within the whole document, then prepending that note to the chunk before it is embedded and before it is added to the keyword index. Anthropic reports a substantial drop in retrieval failures from this step, with further gains when combined with reranking. Prompt caching of the full document keeps the per-chunk generation cost manageable.
body.heading: Restoring context that chunking removes

subtopics.title: Chunking and contextual retrieval

body.body: Fused dense and lexical results are a candidate set, not a final ordering. A reranker, usually a cross-encoder that scores the query and each passage together, is more accurate than embedding similarity because it reads both texts jointly, but it is too slow to run over a whole corpus. The standard arrangement is two stages: retrieve a wide set, on the order of a hundred or more candidates, rerank them, and pass only the top few to the generator. This raises precision in the window and reduces tokens spent on marginal passages, at the price of added latency per query.
body.heading: Adding a second ranking stage

subtopics.title: Hybrid search and reranking

body.body: Exact search compares the query vector with every stored vector, which is accurate but linear in corpus size. Approximate indexes trade a little recall for speed. HNSW builds a layered graph and gives a strong speed and recall balance, with slower builds and more memory; its main knobs are graph connectivity, build-time candidate list size and a query-time search width that raises recall when increased. IVFFlat clusters vectors into lists and probes a subset; it builds faster and uses less memory but should be created after data is loaded. The distance metric, cosine, inner product or Euclidean, must match how the embedding model was trained.
body.heading: Approximate nearest neighbor indexes

body.body: pgvector adds a vector column type, distance operators and both index types to Postgres, keeping embeddings next to relational data with transactions, joins and existing backups. Dedicated engines such as Qdrant organize data into collections of points, each holding one or more vectors plus a JSON payload, and offer payload indexes for filtered search, quantization to shrink memory, sharding and replication. Filtering is the usual deciding factor: tenant or permission filters applied after an approximate search can return too few results, so the engine must combine filter and vector search during traversal.
body.heading: Postgres extension or dedicated engine

subtopics.title: Vector indexes and vector databases

body.body: Evaluate retrieval and generation independently so a failure can be assigned to one of them. For retrieval, build a set of questions with known relevant passages and track recall at k, the share of questions whose needed passage appears in the top k, along with rank-sensitive measures such as mean reciprocal rank. For generation, check faithfulness, meaning every claim is supported by a retrieved passage, and answer relevance. Instruct the model to quote or cite passage ids and to decline when the context does not contain the answer, then verify cited ids exist and support the claim. Enforce document permissions at retrieval time, never by asking the model to withhold text.
body.heading: Measuring the two halves separately

subtopics.title: Grounded generation and retrieval evaluation

concepts.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation supplies a model with relevant passages from an external corpus at request time, so answers are grounded in data the model was never trained on and can cite it. The system has two halves: an offline pipeline that parses, chunks, embeds and indexes documents, and an online path that retrieves, ranks and assembles context for generation. Most quality problems in RAG are retrieval problems, so the engineering effort goes into chunking, search and measurement.
concepts.title: Retrieval-augmented generation with vector databases

modules.intro: This module covers the four building blocks that almost every customer-facing LLM system is assembled from: the model API itself, the prompt and context around it, typed outputs and tools, and retrieval over private data. Each lesson starts from how the mechanism works and ends with how a deployed team operates it under real cost, latency and correctness constraints.
modules.title: LLM Application Building Blocks

code.code:
from agents import Agent, Runner, function_tool

@function_tool
def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> str:
    """Return the shipping status for one order id."""
    return "shipped"

billing = Agent(name="Billing", instructions="Handle refund requests.")

triage = Agent(
    name="Triage",
    instructions="Answer order questions. Hand off refunds to Billing.",
    tools=[lookup_order],
    handoffs=[billing],
)

result = Runner.run_sync(triage, "Where is order 42?", max_turns=6)
print(result.final_output)

concepts.in_practice: A forward deployed team usually begins with the customer's process written as steps, marks which steps are fixed and which need judgement, and builds the fixed parts as a coded workflow with model calls at the judgement points. A full agent loop is introduced only for the open-ended part, with a small tool set, a turn limit and tracing on from day one. The team reads traces daily in the first weeks, fixes tool descriptions before touching prompts, and keeps an eval set of real customer cases so each change to the architecture is compared against the simpler baseline.

sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

body.body: A workflow orchestrates model calls through predefined code paths; an agent lets the model direct its own process and tool usage. Workflows give predictability and are easier to test, agents give flexibility when the number of steps cannot be known in advance. The standard advice is to start with a single well-prompted model call plus retrieval, and add structure only when measurement shows it helps, because every layer of autonomy trades latency and cost for task performance.
body.heading: Two ends of one spectrum

body.body: Five workflow patterns cover most deployments. Prompt chaining splits a task into sequential steps with programmatic checks between them. Routing classifies an input and sends it to a specialized prompt or model. Parallelization runs independent subtasks at once, or runs the same task several times and votes. Orchestrator-workers lets one model break a task down dynamically and delegate pieces. Evaluator-optimizer loops a generator against a critic until criteria are met. Naming the pattern in a design doc makes the control flow reviewable.
body.heading: The named patterns

subtopics.title: Workflows versus agents and the common patterns

body.body: The ReAct formulation interleaves reasoning with actions: the model writes a thought about what it needs, emits an action such as a tool call, receives an observation from the environment, and repeats until it can answer. Reasoning helps the model plan and handle exceptions, while actions ground it in external information instead of its own recall. Modern tool-calling APIs implement the same cycle natively: the model returns a structured tool request, the host executes it, and the result is appended to the conversation for the next turn.
body.heading: How the loop works

body.body: A loop needs explicit stopping conditions: a final answer without tool calls, a maximum number of turns, a token or cost budget, or a human checkpoint. Typical failures are repeated identical tool calls, drifting from the goal as context fills with observations, and compounding errors where one wrong observation steers every later step. Mitigations are concise tool results, clear error messages returned to the model as observations, turn limits, and environment feedback such as test results that give the loop ground truth at each step.
body.heading: Stopping and failure modes

subtopics.title: The reason and act loop

body.body: The OpenAI Agents SDK is a representative example. An Agent is a model configured with a name, instructions, tools and optionally an output type that forces structured final output. A Runner executes the loop: call the model, run requested tools, feed back results, stop on final output or a turn limit. Tools can be plain Python functions whose signature and docstring become the schema, hosted tools, or other agents exposed as tools. Guardrails validate input and output alongside the run, sessions hold conversation history, and built-in tracing records each step.
body.heading: What an SDK gives you

body.body: A handoff transfers control of the conversation to another agent; it is presented to the model as a tool, and the receiving agent sees the history and takes over. Agents as tools keep the calling agent in charge: the sub-agent runs, returns a result, and the caller continues. Use handoffs for triage where a specialist should own the rest of the interaction, and agents as tools when a manager must combine several specialist outputs into one answer.
body.heading: Handoffs versus agents as tools

subtopics.title: Agent SDK primitives: agents, tools, handoffs, runner

body.body: The model only knows a tool through its name, description and parameter schema, so those deserve the same care as the system prompt. Good definitions say when to use the tool, give example inputs, state edge cases, and draw boundaries against similar tools. Choose formats the model writes easily: avoid formats that need exact counts or heavy escaping, prefer absolute identifiers over relative ones, and shape arguments so mistakes are hard to make. Then test by running many example inputs, reading where the model misuses a tool, and rewriting the definition.
body.heading: Tools are prompts

subtopics.title: Designing the agent-computer interface

concepts.summary: An agentic system sits somewhere between a fixed workflow, where code decides the order of model calls, and an autonomous agent, where the model decides its next step in a loop with tools. The engineering skill is choosing the least autonomy that solves the problem, then expressing it with a small set of primitives: instructions, tools, handoffs and a run loop. Agent SDKs package those primitives so the team spends time on tool design and task definition instead of plumbing.
concepts.title: Agent architectures and agentic workflows with agent SDKs

concepts.in_practice: A team typically wraps one customer system per server, starting with three to six read-only tools shaped around the questions agents actually need answered, and adds write tools later behind explicit approval in the host. Development starts on stdio for fast local iteration, then the same server is deployed over Streamable HTTP behind the customer's identity provider so several agents and teams share it. The server lives in the customer's repository with tests and versioned tool schemas, and changes to tool names or descriptions are reviewed like API changes because they alter agent behavior.

sources.title: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

body.body: A host is the AI application the user works in, such as a desktop assistant, an IDE or a custom agent. The host creates one client per server, and each client holds a dedicated connection to that server. A server is a program that provides context and capabilities. Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 requests, responses and notifications. A connection starts with an initialize exchange in which both sides state protocol version and capabilities, so each knows which features the other supports before any tool is listed or called.
body.heading: The three roles

body.body: Two standard transports exist. With stdio, the host launches the server as a subprocess and exchanges messages over standard input and output; this suits local tools and gives the server the user's local permissions. With Streamable HTTP, the server runs as an independent service that handles many clients over HTTP, optionally streaming server messages; this suits shared, remotely hosted integrations and is where authorization matters. The message format is identical in both, so server logic does not change with the transport.
body.heading: Transports

subtopics.title: Hosts, clients, servers and the protocol lifecycle

body.body: Tools are functions the model may call, each with a name, description and JSON Schema for inputs; they are model-controlled and can have side effects. Resources are data identified by URI that the application can read and place in context, such as a file, a record or a schema; they are application-controlled. Prompts are reusable templates the user selects, such as a slash command. Clients discover each with list requests and are told about changes through notifications. Picking the right primitive matters: read-only reference data is usually a resource, an action is a tool.
body.heading: Server primitives

body.body: The protocol also lets servers ask things of the client. Sampling lets a server request a model completion through the host, so the server needs no model key of its own. Roots tell a server which filesystem or URI boundaries it should work within. Elicitation lets a server ask the user for additional information mid-operation. Hosts vary in which of these they support, so a server should check negotiated capabilities and degrade gracefully instead of assuming every feature exists.
body.heading: Client features

subtopics.title: Tools, resources and prompts

body.body: The official SDKs remove most protocol work. In the Python SDK, the FastMCP class turns decorated functions into tools: type hints become the input schema and the docstring becomes the description the model reads. Resources are declared with a URI template and prompts with another decorator. A practical rule for stdio servers is never to write to standard output except protocol messages, because stray prints corrupt the JSON-RPC stream; log to standard error or a file. Return compact, structured results and clear error text, since the model reads both.
body.heading: From function to tool

body.body: Test a server at three levels: unit tests on the underlying functions, protocol-level checks with an inspector tool that lists and calls tools interactively, and end-to-end runs in a real host to see whether the model picks the right tool. The reference servers repository shows idiomatic implementations for filesystems, git, fetch and memory and is a useful base for conventions. Keep the tool count small and task-shaped; a server that mirrors every REST endpoint gives the model too many near-identical choices.
body.heading: Testing and reuse

subtopics.title: Building a server with an SDK

body.body: The specification puts user consent and control at the center: users should understand and approve what data is shared and which tools run, and hosts should treat tool descriptions from untrusted servers as untrusted. For HTTP transports the specification defines an authorization flow based on OAuth, so a remote server acts as a protected resource and validates tokens issued for it. For stdio servers, credentials come from the environment. In both cases apply least privilege: scope tokens narrowly, separate read tools from write tools, validate every argument server-side, and log each call for audit.
body.heading: Security model

subtopics.title: Trust, authorization and deployment

concepts.summary: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard for connecting AI applications to external systems, so one integration works across many hosts instead of being rewritten per agent framework. A server exposes tools, resources and prompts over JSON-RPC; a host application runs clients that discover and call them. For a forward deployed engineer, an MCP server is often the cleanest way to hand a customer's internal systems to an agent with a clear contract and a clear trust boundary.
concepts.title: Building Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers

concepts.in_practice: Teams usually pick the durability layer from what the customer already runs: a workflow engine where one exists, a checkpointed graph framework backed by Postgres otherwise. The agent loop is written so every model and tool call is a recorded step with a timeout, a retry policy and an idempotency key, and human approval is a durable wait instead of a blocking request. Before go-live the team kills workers mid-run, replays histories against new code, and uses gradual rollouts so agents already in flight finish on the version they started on.

sources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
OpenAI Agents SDK: Orchestrating multiple agents

body.body: There are two ways to coordinate agents. In model-driven orchestration, a lead agent plans, decides which specialists to invoke and synthesizes results; this adapts to open-ended tasks. In code-driven orchestration, the program fixes the flow: chain agents so one output feeds the next, branch on a structured classification, run independent agents in parallel, or loop a worker with an evaluator. Code-driven flows are more predictable in speed, cost and behavior. Most production systems mix them, with code owning the outer flow and a model deciding inside bounded steps.
body.heading: Model-driven versus code-driven

body.body: In the orchestrator-worker design used for research systems, a lead agent decomposes a query and spawns subagents that work in parallel, each with its own context window, returning condensed findings. This buys breadth and context isolation at a price: multi-agent runs consume several times more tokens than a single agent, so they fit high-value, parallelizable tasks. Delegation quality decides the outcome. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources, and clear task boundaries, otherwise workers duplicate effort or leave gaps.
body.heading: Orchestrator and subagents

subtopics.title: Multi-agent orchestration patterns

body.body: In Temporal, a workflow is code whose progress is recorded as an event history. Anything with side effects, such as a model call, a tool call or a database write, runs as an activity whose result is stored. If a worker dies, another worker replays the workflow code against the history, reusing recorded activity results until it reaches the point of failure, then continues. This requires workflow code to be deterministic: no direct network calls, random values or wall-clock reads inside the workflow function. Timers and waits for external signals are durable too, so a run can pause for days.
body.heading: How durable execution works

body.body: For an agent, the loop is the workflow and each model call and tool call is an activity with its own timeout and retry policy. The nondeterministic model output is safe because it is recorded once and replayed from history. Long conversations make histories large, so engines provide a way to continue as a fresh run carrying forward summarized state. Changing workflow code while runs are in flight needs versioning, because replay of an old history against new code must take the same branches.
body.heading: Mapping agents onto it

subtopics.title: Workflow engines and replay

body.body: Engines give at-least-once activity execution, so every side-effecting tool needs an idempotency key derived from the run and step, passed through to the downstream system. Agent-specific additions: classify errors so a malformed tool argument is returned to the model as an observation while a rate limit is retried with backoff by the engine; set heartbeats on long activities so stalls are detected; and treat token spend as a resource checked before each model activity, with the run failing closed when the cap is reached.
body.heading: Beyond the basics

subtopics.title: Idempotency, retries and budget control

body.body: LangGraph models an agent system as a graph of nodes that read and update a shared typed state, with edges, including conditional ones, deciding what runs next. A checkpointer persists state after each step under a thread identifier, backed by a store such as Postgres. That gives resumption after failure, inspection of any earlier state, and the ability to fork a run from a past checkpoint for debugging. A node can interrupt the run to wait for a person; the graph resumes later with the human's input merged into state, which is how approval steps and edits are implemented.
body.heading: Checkpointed graphs

subtopics.title: Graph state, checkpoints and human approval

concepts.summary: Orchestration decides which agent or step runs next and what context it receives; durable execution makes sure a long run survives crashes, deploys and rate limits without losing or repeating work. Agent runs are long, expensive and stateful, so a failure halfway through cannot simply restart from the top. The lesson covers multi-agent coordination patterns, then the workflow engines and checkpointing frameworks that give those patterns reliable state.
concepts.title: Agent orchestration and durable execution

concepts.in_practice: On a customer engagement the eval set is agreed with the customer early, because it doubles as the acceptance definition for the pilot. The team collects a few dozen real cases with the customer's domain expert, writes code assertions first, adds a calibrated model judge for the qualities code cannot check, and wires both into CI so every prompt or tool change shows a before and after. During the pilot someone reviews a sample of traces each week with the expert, adds new failure cases to the set, and reports pass rates by failure category instead of one headline score.

sources.title: Claude Docs: Create strong empirical evaluations

body.body: Criteria should be specific, measurable and tied to the customer's task, usually several at once: task accuracy, format validity, tone, latency, cost per case. Build the set from the real task distribution plus deliberate edge cases such as ambiguous input, irrelevant input and very long input. Volume with automated grading generally beats a small hand-graded set. Models can generate additional cases from a seed set, which a person then spot-checks for realism.
body.heading: What goes beyond a gold set

subtopics.title: Success criteria and test sets

body.body: Use the fastest reliable grader that fits. Code-based grading, such as exact match, string or regex checks and schema validation, is cheap and deterministic. Model-based grading handles nuance: give the judge a detailed rubric, ask it to reason before deciding, and force a constrained verdict such as pass or fail or a short scale. Human grading is the most flexible and the slowest, so reserve it for calibration.
body.heading: Choosing a grader

body.body: A model judge is itself a system that needs evaluation. Have a domain expert label a sample with pass or fail and a written critique, run the judge on the same sample, and measure agreement; revise the rubric until the two align, then re-check periodically. Binary judgements with reasons are easier to align than numeric scores. Where possible use a different model from the one being graded, and keep judge prompts in version control with the eval results they produced.
body.heading: Keeping a judge honest

subtopics.title: Code, model and human graders

body.body: An agent can reach a right answer by a wasteful or unsafe path, or a wrong answer after correct steps, so grade at several levels. Outcome checks inspect final state: was the ticket created with the right fields, did the record change as intended. Trajectory checks inspect the trace: were the expected tools called with valid arguments, were forbidden tools avoided, how many turns and tokens were used. Component checks isolate one step, such as routing accuracy or retrieval quality. Prefer outcome checks where several valid paths exist, since strict step matching penalizes legitimate alternatives.
body.heading: What to measure

body.body: Agent evals need a controlled environment: seeded test data, sandboxed or mocked tools with realistic responses, and reset between cases so runs are independent. Because agent behavior varies between runs, repeat each case several times and report a pass rate instead of a single result. Multi-turn tasks need a simulated user, often another model following a scripted persona and goal. Store full traces with each result so a failing case can be opened and read step by step.
body.heading: Harness needs

subtopics.title: Evaluating agent trajectories

body.body: The highest-value activity is reading traces. Sample real or pilot interactions, write a short note on what went wrong in each, group the notes into failure categories, and count them; the largest category sets the next piece of work. Each confirmed failure becomes a regression case. Unit-style assertions run on every change in CI, model-graded suites run on a schedule or before release, and a sample of production traffic is scored continuously to catch drift. A simple viewer that shows the trace beside the grade removes friction and gets domain experts involved.
body.heading: From traces to tests

subtopics.title: Error analysis and evals in the delivery loop

concepts.summary: Evaluation turns a vague sense that the system seems fine into a number tied to defined success criteria, so prompts, models and architectures can be changed with evidence. A working eval practice has three layers: fast assertions in code, model-graded and human-graded quality checks, and measurement on real usage. For agents the unit under test is the whole trajectory and the final state of the world, not only the last message.
concepts.title: Evaluating LLM and agent systems

concepts.in_practice: A deployment team threat-models the agent with the customer's security group early, walking the OWASP list against the actual data flows and tool permissions and recording each risk with an owner. Controls are then built as code around the model, not as prompt text alone: input and output filters, scoped credentials, approval steps and audit logging, each covered by adversarial test cases that run in CI. The resulting evidence pack of risk register, eval results and monitoring plan is what the customer's governance board signs off, and it is updated whenever a tool, model or data source changes.

sources.title: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications
OWASP GenAI Security Project: LLM Top 10
Claude Docs: Mitigate jailbreaks and prompt injections

body.body: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a voluntary framework for managing risks of AI systems to individuals, organizations and society. Its core has four functions. Govern establishes policies, roles and accountability across the organization. Map sets the context: intended use, affected people, and where harm could arise. Measure assesses and tracks identified risks with quantitative and qualitative methods. Manage prioritizes and acts on them, including monitoring and incident response. A companion profile addresses generative AI specifically. The framework describes trustworthy systems as valid and reliable, safe, secure and resilient, accountable and transparent, explainable, privacy-enhanced and fair.
body.heading: The four functions

body.body: Customers in regulated industries often structure their AI review around these functions, so it helps to deliver artifacts that map to them: a use-case description with intended and out-of-scope uses, a risk register with owner and mitigation per risk, evaluation results as measurement evidence, and a monitoring and escalation plan. A customer impact assessment asks who is affected by a wrong or harmful output, how they would find out, and what recourse exists. Writing this alongside the design doc is cheaper than retrofitting it at review time.
body.heading: Using it on an engagement

subtopics.title: Risk management with the NIST AI RMF

body.body: The OWASP list is the common vocabulary for security review of model-backed applications. It covers prompt injection, direct and indirect; sensitive information disclosure; supply chain weaknesses in models, data and dependencies; data and model poisoning; improper handling of model output by downstream code; excessive agency, where a system has more functionality, permission or autonomy than the task needs; system prompt leakage; weaknesses in vector and embedding stores; misinformation and overreliance; and unbounded consumption of resources. Each entry lists example scenarios and mitigations.
body.heading: The threat list

body.body: Three entries dominate agent designs. Indirect prompt injection arrives through content the agent reads, such as a web page, a document or a tool result, so all retrieved content is untrusted input. Improper output handling means model output must be validated and encoded before it reaches a shell, a query or a browser. Excessive agency is addressed by design: minimal tool sets, narrowly scoped credentials, authorization checks in the downstream system instead of in the prompt, and human approval for high-impact actions.
body.heading: Reading it for agents

subtopics.title: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications

body.body: No single control stops adversarial input, so controls are stacked. Screen inputs with a lightweight model or classifier before the main call. Validate inputs for known attack patterns. Write system prompts that state the role, the boundaries and how to respond to out-of-scope requests. Separate instructions from untrusted content with clear delimiters and tell the model that delimited content is data. Check outputs before returning or acting on them. Monitor continuously: log refusals and flagged inputs, look for repeat offenders, and throttle or block accounts that probe repeatedly.
body.heading: Defense in depth

body.body: Guardrails need their own evals. Maintain a red-team set of known jailbreak and injection attempts alongside a set of benign inputs that resemble attacks, and measure both the block rate and the false-positive rate, since an overly strict filter breaks legitimate use. Include indirect cases where the malicious instruction is planted in a retrieved document or a tool response. Rerun the set on every prompt or model change, and add each real incident as a new case.
body.heading: Testing the controls

subtopics.title: Layered defenses against jailbreaks and prompt injection

body.body: Beyond redacting data before the model sees it and gating mutations behind a person, production reviews expect the surrounding record: a data-flow map showing which fields reach which model provider and under what retention terms, per-user authorization so an agent never retrieves what its user could not, audit logs linking each action to a user, a run and an approver, and a documented way to disable a tool or the whole agent quickly.
body.heading: What to add around the core controls

subtopics.title: Privacy, least privilege and human approval

concepts.summary: Responsible AI work combines a governance process that identifies and tracks risk with technical controls that limit what a model-driven system can see, say and do. Frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework give the process; the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications gives the threat list; layered guardrails give the enforcement. In customer deployments this is what gets a system through risk review and keeps it there.
concepts.title: Responsible AI controls and guardrails

deduped = df.drop_duplicates(subset=['email_clean'], keep='first')

concepts.in_practice: A forward deployed team usually gets a sample export in week one, profiles it in a notebook, and returns a short findings document with null rates, duplicate estimates and open questions for the data owner. The mapping spec and crosswalks live in a shared sheet or repo the customer can edit. Normalization and matching run as versioned pipeline steps, not one-off scripts, with a review queue for uncertain pairs staffed by someone on the customer side who knows the domain. Every merge is logged with its evidence, a labeled sample is kept as a regression set, and match quality is reported alongside pipeline health so data owners see drift when a new source is onboarded.

sources.title: pandas User Guide: Working with missing data

body.body: Start every engagement by measuring the data, not by reading its documentation. For each column compute the null rate, distinct count, top values, min and max, and string length distribution. In pandas, isna and notna detect missing values, and the library uses different sentinels by dtype: NaN for floats, NaT for datetimes, and NA for the nullable extension dtypes such as Int64, boolean and string. Loading an integer column with gaps silently converts it to float unless a nullable dtype is requested, which breaks identifiers. Also look for disguised nulls: empty strings, N/A, 0000-00-00, or a placeholder contact name reused thousands of times.
body.heading: Profile before you transform

body.body: Missing data has three honest treatments: drop the row with dropna, fill it with fillna or interpolate, or keep it missing and let consumers handle it. The right choice depends on meaning. A missing discount can be zero; a missing birth date cannot be guessed. Comparisons with NA propagate as unknown rather than False, so filters can quietly drop rows. Record each rule in a short data contract the customer signs off on.
body.heading: Decide per column, and write it down

subtopics.title: Profiling an unknown extract and handling missing values

body.body: A data mapping is a table with one row per target field: source system, source path, type, transformation rule, default, and owner. For JSON and XML payloads the source path is a JSONPath or XPath expression, and the spec must say what happens with repeated elements, namespaces, and optional nodes. Enumerations need crosswalk tables, for example mapping five spellings of a status code from three systems onto one canonical value. Keep crosswalks as data, not as CASE statements buried in code, so the customer can review and extend them.
body.heading: The mapping spec is the deliverable

body.body: Watch for fields with the same name and different meaning across systems, local time stored without a zone, currency without a code, free-text fields carrying structured data, and identifiers that were recycled. Always carry the source system and source primary key through to the target so any record can be traced back. Validate the mapping by reconciling row counts and control totals between source and target.
body.heading: Common traps

subtopics.title: Data mapping: source-to-target specs and crosswalks

body.body: Most duplicates disappear once values are put in a canonical form. Trim and collapse whitespace, case-fold, strip punctuation and diacritics, parse phone numbers to a single international format, lower-case email addresses, parse dates to ISO form, and standardize addresses and company suffixes. Keep the raw value next to the cleaned one. In pandas, duplicated flags repeated rows over a chosen subset of columns and drop_duplicates removes them with a keep policy; index uniqueness can be checked with is_unique and enforced by disallowing duplicate labels. OpenRefine does the same work interactively, with facets to see value distributions and key-collision clustering that groups variants such as differently ordered or punctuated names, and it records every operation as a replayable history.
body.heading: Standardize, then compare

subtopics.title: Normalization and deterministic deduplication

body.body: When no shared identifier exists, records must be linked on fuzzy evidence: a similar name, the same birth date, a nearby address. The Fellegi-Sunter model treats each field comparison as evidence. For each comparison level it estimates m, the probability of that outcome among true matches, and u, the probability among non-matches. Their ratio gives a match weight, and the weights sum to an overall match probability. Agreement on a rare surname counts for more than agreement on a common one when term frequency adjustments are enabled.
body.heading: Why exact keys are not enough

body.body: Comparing every pair is quadratic, so blocking rules restrict candidate pairs to those sharing something cheap, such as the first letters of a surname plus birth year. Use several blocking rules so one typo does not hide a match. Splink implements this workflow in SQL over backends such as DuckDB and Spark, estimates parameters without labeled data using expectation maximization, and provides charts to inspect weights. Pairs above a threshold are clustered into entities using connected components.
body.heading: Making it scale

body.body: Set two thresholds, not one: auto-merge above the upper, reject below the lower, and send the band between to human review. Measure precision and recall on a labeled sample the customer helped create, because the cost of a false merge is usually much higher than a missed one.
body.heading: Choosing thresholds

subtopics.title: Probabilistic record linkage with blocking and match weights

body.body: Once records are clustered, survivorship rules pick the value for each field of the golden record: most trusted source, most recent update, most complete value, or majority vote. Rules are set per field, since the billing system may win for address while the CRM wins for contact name. Never destroy the inputs. Keep a link table from each source record to its entity id, with the rule and score that put it there, so a wrong merge can be split and the entity rebuilt. Assign stable entity ids so downstream joins survive reruns, and version the matching model so changes in clustering can be explained.
body.heading: From clusters to one record

subtopics.title: Survivorship, golden records and reversibility

concepts.summary: Customer data arrives as overlapping exports from CRMs, ERPs and spreadsheets, with inconsistent formats, missing values and the same real-world entity recorded many times. The work is to profile it, map it onto a target schema, normalize it, and then decide which records refer to the same entity. Done well, this yields a traceable, reversible set of golden records that downstream AI features can trust.

concepts.in_practice: On arrival the team requests a service identity, a scoped role, a sandbox schema and a small dedicated warehouse or job cluster, then spends the first days exploring metadata and query history with a customer analyst on call. Findings go into a short data map listing trusted tables, their grain, owners and refresh times. Development happens in the sandbox schema against production data read-only, with cost monitored per warehouse or cluster tag. Before go-live the customer's platform team reviews grants, network configuration and expected monthly spend, and production jobs run under the service identity, not under an engineer's personal login.

body.body: Snowflake is a managed service with three layers. Storage holds data in a compressed, columnar internal format that Snowflake reorganizes and manages; you reach it only through SQL. Compute is provided by virtual warehouses, independent clusters that each run queries without sharing compute with other warehouses, so a heavy load job does not slow a dashboard. The cloud services layer coordinates everything: authentication, access control, metadata, query parsing and optimization. The design is a hybrid of shared-disk, with one central data repository, and shared-nothing, with massively parallel compute clusters.
body.heading: Three layers

body.body: Cost follows warehouse size and running time, so ask which warehouse you may use, set auto-suspend, and avoid leaving it running for an idle service. Scale up for a complex query, scale out for concurrency. Since each warehouse is isolated, request a dedicated one for your workload so its spend and performance are attributable.
body.heading: What it means on an engagement

subtopics.title: Snowflake architecture: storage, virtual warehouses, cloud services

body.body: Databricks is a unified platform for data engineering, analytics and AI, built around the lakehouse idea: data sits in the customer's own cloud object storage in open table formats such as Delta Lake, and managed compute reads it in place. A workspace is the working environment holding notebooks, jobs, SQL editors and dashboards. Compute comes in several forms: all-purpose clusters for interactive notebooks, job compute that starts for a scheduled run and stops, SQL warehouses for BI-style queries, and serverless options. Unity Catalog provides governance with a three-level namespace of catalog, schema and table.
body.heading: Open storage with a unified platform

body.body: Expect to work in Python and SQL side by side, with Spark DataFrames for large data. Since files live in the customer's bucket, network paths, storage credentials and table maintenance matter more than in a fully managed warehouse. Choose job compute for production runs; interactive clusters are for development.
body.heading: Practical differences from a warehouse

subtopics.title: Databricks: the lakehouse, workspaces and compute

body.body: Both platforms use role-based access control, with privileges granted on securable objects to roles or groups, never to individuals where it can be avoided. Request a dedicated service principal or service user for your application, a role with read access to named schemas only, a separate schema where you may create objects, and a dedicated compute resource. Prefer key-pair or OAuth authentication to passwords. Sensitive columns may be protected by masking policies and row-level filters, which means the same query returns different results for different roles; confirm which role production will run as before validating outputs.
body.heading: Ask for the narrowest working grant

body.body: Establish whether data may leave the platform, whether model calls to an external provider are permitted for these columns, what region the data must stay in, and who approves new grants. Access requests often take longer than the build, so file them on day one.
body.heading: Governance questions to settle early

subtopics.title: Access, roles and governance in an account you do not own

body.body: Documentation is usually stale, but metadata is not. Query the information schema for tables, columns, types and row counts, and sort by last altered time to separate live tables from abandoned ones. Query history shows which tables people and tools really read, how they join them, and which filters they apply; the most frequent queries from the BI service account are the best guide to trusted tables. Lineage views, where enabled, show which jobs write each table. Look at view definitions and existing dbt or notebook code before writing your own logic.
body.heading: Use the platform's own metadata

body.body: For a candidate table, check grain by counting rows against distinct keys, check freshness by the maximum load timestamp, and reconcile one known total, such as last month's revenue, against a number the business already reports. Write down what you learn; it often becomes the customer's first real data dictionary.
body.heading: Verify before you trust

subtopics.title: Finding your way in an undocumented warehouse

body.body: Customers often prefer that data never leaves their governed platform. Both vendors offer ways to do that: Databricks positions itself as a platform for building and deploying AI alongside data, with model serving, vector search and experiment tracking in the workspace, and Snowflake offers in-account functions and container-based compute for similar purposes. The alternative is an external application that queries the platform through a driver or SQL API and calls models elsewhere. The first keeps governance simple and reuses existing permissions; the second gives more control over models, latency and tooling. Decide with the customer's security team, and whichever path is chosen, read from curated tables with a dedicated role, never from raw landing zones.
body.heading: Bring the model to the data when you can

subtopics.title: Running AI workloads next to the data

concepts.summary: Most enterprise customers already keep their analytical data in Snowflake or Databricks, so AI work starts inside an account someone else owns and governs. Both platforms separate storage from compute, but they differ in how compute is provisioned, how data is stored, and how access is granted. A forward deployed engineer needs to read the architecture quickly, work within the customer's roles and budgets, and find the right tables in a warehouse nobody documented.
concepts.title: Working in customer data platforms: Snowflake and Databricks

concepts.in_practice: A team keeps the dbt project in git with one branch per change. Each developer builds into a personal schema, and a pull request triggers a CI job that builds only modified models and their dependents in a temporary schema and runs their tests. Merges deploy to production, where a scheduler or orchestrator runs the build after ingestion completes. On customer engagements the first weeks often go into staging models and tests over existing raw tables, which surface inconsistencies quickly and give the customer a documented, tested base that outlives the engagement. Test failures route to a channel with a named owner, and generated docs with lineage are published for analysts.

sources.title: dbt: Add data tests to your DAG
dbt: How we structure our dbt projects

body.body: Older ETL tools transformed data on a separate server before loading it. Cheap, elastic warehouse compute reversed the order: an ingestion tool lands raw data unchanged, and transformations run as SQL in the warehouse, where they are easy to inspect and rerun. dbt handles only the T. It does not extract or load data, and it does not hold data itself; it compiles your project into SQL and sends it to the platform through an adapter for Snowflake, Databricks, BigQuery, Postgres and others. The open-source dbt Core runs from the command line, and the hosted dbt platform adds scheduling, an IDE and a catalog.
body.heading: Transform inside the warehouse

body.body: Transformations become reviewable code in git, not logic hidden in BI tools or stored procedures. A new engineer can read the project, see lineage, and trust tested models, which is exactly what a handover to the customer's team requires.
body.heading: Why it matters for customer work

subtopics.title: ELT and where dbt fits

body.body: A SQL model is one file containing one select statement; the file name becomes the model name. You never write create table or insert statements, because dbt wraps the select according to the configured materialization. Reference another model with the ref function and raw tables with the source function. dbt uses those references to build a directed acyclic graph, run models in dependency order, and resolve the correct schema for each environment, so the same code builds into a developer's sandbox or into production. Models can also be written in Python on platforms that support it.
body.heading: A model is a select statement

body.body: View is the default and stores only the query. Table rebuilds the whole result each run. Incremental processes only new or changed rows, which is necessary for large fact tables but requires a reliable unique key and filter. Ephemeral models are inlined as common table expressions. Start with views and tables, and move to incremental only when build time demands it.
body.heading: Materializations

subtopics.title: Models, ref, sources and materializations

body.body: The recommended structure moves data from source-conformed to business-conformed shapes. Staging models map one to one onto source tables and do only light work: renaming, type casting, basic computations and categorization. They are the single place each raw table is touched. Intermediate models combine staging models into purpose-built steps, such as pivoting payments or joining order lines, and are usually not exposed to end users. Marts are the wide, entity-grained tables that consumers query, organized by business area, for example customers and orders in a finance or marketing folder.
body.heading: Three layers with distinct jobs

body.body: Use consistent prefixes such as stg, int, fct and dim, keep folder structure aligned with the layers, and set materialization defaults per folder in the project file. The discipline matters most in a messy warehouse: fixes to a source quirk are made once in staging, and every downstream model inherits them.
body.heading: Conventions that pay off

subtopics.title: Project structure: staging, intermediate, marts

body.body: A dbt data test is a query that returns failing rows; zero rows means the test passes. Generic tests are parameterized and declared in YAML on a model or column. Four ship with dbt: unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships, the last checking referential integrity to another model. Singular tests are one-off SQL files in the tests directory for a specific rule, such as no order having a negative total. You can write your own generic tests and install packages of them. Severity can be set to warn or error, and failing rows can be stored for inspection.
body.heading: Assertions that run against real data

body.body: Put unique and not_null on the primary key of every model, relationships on foreign keys in marts, and accepted_values on status columns. Add source freshness checks so stale loads are caught before models run. The build command runs models and tests together in graph order and skips downstream models when an upstream test fails.
body.heading: What to test first

subtopics.title: Data tests

concepts.summary: In ELT, raw data is loaded into the warehouse first and transformed there with SQL. dbt is the standard tool for that transformation step: each model is a select statement, dbt works out the dependency graph, builds the tables and views in order, and runs tests against the results. It brings software engineering practice, meaning version control, modularity, testing and documentation, to analytics code.
concepts.title: ELT transformations with dbt

concepts.in_practice: A typical customer pipeline has an ingestion step landing raw files or tables, a dbt build triggered when ingestion succeeds, then Python steps for entity resolution, embedding or model scoring, and finally a publish step with quality checks. The team develops locally against a small sample, tests task logic as plain functions, and ships DAG or asset code through pull requests into the customer's deployment. Each step is idempotent per partition so on-call engineers can clear and rerun safely. Failures alert a shared channel with a runbook link, and the handover includes the schedule, owners, expected runtimes and the procedure for backfilling after a fix.

body.body: An Airflow installation has a scheduler that triggers scheduled workflows and submits tasks to an executor, a DAG processor that parses DAG files, a web interface and API for inspecting and triggering runs, and a metadata database that stores the state of every DAG run and task instance. The executor decides where tasks run: locally in small setups, or on remote workers through Celery or Kubernetes in production. An optional triggerer handles deferred tasks that wait on external events without occupying a worker. DAG files are plain Python that all components must be able to read.
body.heading: Components

body.body: A DAG declares tasks and their dependencies plus a schedule. A task is an instance of an operator, a template for a unit of work such as running a bash command, a Python function or a SQL statement; sensors wait for a condition. Airflow orchestrates; heavy computation should run in the warehouse or a separate compute service, not in the worker process.
body.heading: DAGs, tasks and operators

subtopics.title: Airflow architecture and core concepts

body.body: Orchestrators retry and backfill, so a task must give the same result when run twice for the same interval. Parameterize work by the run's logical date and data interval, never by the wall clock. Write with overwrite-partition or merge semantics, not blind appends. Set retries and retry delay in default arguments, add timeouts, and keep tasks small enough that a retry is cheap. Pass only small values between tasks through XCom; put real data in storage and pass its location. Keep top-level DAG file code light, because the file is parsed repeatedly. Decide deliberately whether catchup should create runs for past intervals, and use backfill to reprocess history after a logic fix.
body.heading: Design each task to be rerun

subtopics.title: Authoring DAGs: idempotency, retries and backfills

body.body: Dagster's central abstraction is the asset: an object in persistent storage, such as a table, file or trained model, defined in code by a function that produces it. Decorating a function as an asset declares the thing, and naming other assets as its inputs declares dependencies, so the lineage graph comes from the code itself and no separate wiring is needed. Dagster then materializes assets, records metadata about each materialization, and shows which assets are stale relative to their upstream. Partitions, schedules, sensors and asset checks attach to assets.
body.heading: Declare what should exist

body.body: Because assets are ordinary Python functions with resources injected, they can be unit tested and run locally with a development server before deployment. The asset graph also answers the questions customers ask most: where does this table come from, and when was it last refreshed. Integrations can load dbt models as assets, so SQL transformations and Python steps share one lineage view.
body.heading: Consequences for development

subtopics.title: Dagster and the asset model

body.body: The deciding factor on an engagement is rarely features. If the customer has Airflow with an on-call rotation, add a DAG there, even if you would pick differently on a blank slate. Task-centric Airflow suits heterogeneous jobs across many systems and has the largest ecosystem of provider packages and managed offerings. Asset-centric Dagster suits teams that think in tables and want lineage, local testing and data quality checks built in. Prefect is a third common option with a Python-first flow model.
body.heading: Default to what the customer runs

body.body: Whichever tool is used, plan for secrets held in connections or a secrets backend, never in code; alerting on failure and on missed service-level targets; concurrency limits so backfills do not overload the warehouse; and deployment of pipeline code through CI. Event-driven triggers from queues such as Kafka, SQS or Pub/Sub complement schedules when data arrives irregularly, and columnar files such as Parquet are the usual interchange format between steps.
body.heading: Operating concerns

subtopics.title: Choosing an orchestrator and operating it

concepts.summary: An orchestrator schedules pipeline steps, runs them in dependency order, retries failures and records what happened. Airflow models a pipeline as a DAG of tasks and is the tool most customers already run; Dagster models it as a graph of data assets and is common in newer stacks. Knowing both lets a forward deployed engineer extend whatever the customer has, without introducing another system.
concepts.title: Data pipeline orchestration with Airflow and Dagster
