They deploy a thin end-to-end slice with the customer's infrastructure tool and pipeline, using workload identity and the cloud-native model endpoint the customer has already approved. The design document states the deployment model, what data crosses the boundary, and how upgrades and rollbacks are done, phrased against the provider's architecture framework so the review board can sign off. Only after that slice works do they add the real workload and sizing.

sources.title: Azure Architecture Center: Application architecture guide

body.body: A vendor-hosted deployment runs in your company's cloud and the customer reaches it over an API; you keep full operational control but customer data leaves their boundary. A customer-cloud deployment, often called bring your own cloud, runs your software in an account, project or subscription the customer owns; data stays put, but you operate through whatever access they grant. An on-premises deployment runs on customer hardware, often with no managed services at all. Each step toward the customer removes things you rely on: managed databases, your own observability stack, the ability to push a fix in minutes. Decide the model during scoping, because it determines packaging, the upgrade path, who is on call, and whether a hosted model API is even reachable.
body.heading: Three shapes and what each costs you

body.body: A common compromise keeps a small control plane with the vendor (release metadata, licensing, configuration, fleet health) and puts the data plane, which touches customer data and calls models, inside the customer account. The data plane opens outbound connections to the control plane, so the customer does not have to open inbound access. This gives you visibility and a controlled upgrade channel while customer data stays inside their boundary. Be explicit in the design document about what crosses the boundary: usually versions, health signals and aggregate metrics, never prompts, documents or records.
body.heading: Control plane and data plane split

subtopics.title: Deployment models: vendor-hosted, customer cloud, on-premises

body.body: On AWS, IAM controls who is authenticated and what they are authorized to do, and the standard way into a customer account is a role they create that trusts a principal in your account. You assume it and receive temporary credentials, so nobody exchanges long-lived access keys. The trust policy says who may assume the role; the permission policy says what the role may do. Google Cloud uses service accounts with impersonation and workload identity federation for the same purpose; Azure uses Entra ID service principals and managed identities with role assignments at subscription or resource group scope. In every cloud, ask for a named role with a written permission list, scoped to the resources the deployment creates, and expect the customer security team to review it line by line.
body.heading: Roles instead of shared credentials

body.body: Access for humans and access for running workloads are separate problems. A workload should obtain credentials from the platform at run time: an instance or task role on AWS, a service account bound to a Kubernetes service account on Google Cloud, a managed identity on Azure. This removes static secrets from images and configuration, and it lets the customer audit every call the workload makes in their own logs. When the customer asks what your software can touch, the answer should be one role and its policy.
body.heading: Workload identity

subtopics.title: Identity and access across the customer boundary

body.body: In a customer account the infrastructure definition is a deliverable, not an internal tool. Customers typically standardize on one tool and expect a module they can read, pin to a version, and apply through their own pipeline with their own state backend. Keep inputs few and explicit (network identifiers, key identifiers, sizing), avoid creating account-wide resources, tag everything so cost and ownership are traceable, and document a clean destroy path. Expect policy checks in their pipeline to reject public endpoints, unencrypted storage and wildcard permissions.
body.heading: Shipping modules, not console steps

subtopics.title: Infrastructure as code that the customer can run

body.body: The tenancy unit differs: an AWS account, a Google Cloud project inside a folder and organization, an Azure subscription containing resource groups. Managed Kubernetes is EKS, GKE and AKS. Object storage is S3, Cloud Storage and Blob Storage. Managed Postgres, queues, secret stores and key management exist in all three. Hosted model access is commonly Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI and Azure OpenAI or Azure AI Foundry, and many customers will only approve the one inside their existing cloud agreement. Keep cloud-specific code behind thin interfaces for storage, queues, secrets and model calls, and standardize on portable pieces such as containers, Postgres and Kubernetes where the customer allows it.
body.heading: Same building blocks, different names and boundaries

body.body: Each provider publishes architecture guidance that customer review boards cite. The AWS Well-Architected Framework organizes review questions into pillars: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. The Azure Architecture Center application architecture guide walks through architecture styles, technology choices and design principles. You do not need to memorize them, but writing your design document in their vocabulary shortens reviews, because the reviewer can map your answers to the checklist they already use.
body.heading: Using the architecture frameworks

subtopics.title: Mapping one architecture onto AWS, Google Cloud and Azure

The goal is to get from a signed contract to a first working deployment without waiting weeks on access.

concepts.in_practice: A team keeps a single release pipeline that produces signed images and a versioned chart, plus a small set of per-customer values files that contain no secrets. Each customer environment pulls a pinned release, either through the customer's own pipeline or through a GitOps controller in the cluster, and secrets come from the customer's secret store. Short event-driven pieces run as functions; the agent runtime and anything streaming or long-lived runs as containers. Release notes list configuration changes explicitly, because the person applying the upgrade is often a customer platform engineer.

body.body: A customer will usually mirror your images into their own registry and scan them before anything runs. That makes image hygiene a delivery concern: small base images, no secrets in layers, a non-root user, a published software bill of materials, and signatures the customer can verify. Reference images by digest in manifests so the mirrored copy is provably the one you tested. Build for the CPU architecture they run, and keep the registry host a configurable value everywhere.
body.heading: What changes when the registry is not yours

subtopics.title: Images as the unit of delivery

body.body: Kubernetes gives you declarative deployment, service discovery, rollouts and self-healing, but a customer cluster arrives with its own admission policies, ingress controller, storage classes and quotas. Ship a chart whose values expose those choices: ingress class, storage class, resource requests, node selectors, image registry, and existing secret names. Request namespace-scoped permissions where possible, since cluster-wide roles and custom resource definitions trigger extra review. Test the chart on a locked-down cluster before the customer does.
body.heading: A chart that survives someone else's cluster

subtopics.title: Packaging for a customer Kubernetes cluster

body.body: Split the pipeline at the artifact. Your side builds, tests, scans and signs a versioned release; the customer side pulls that release and promotes it through their environments under their change process. Authenticate pipelines to clouds with short-lived federated tokens rather than stored keys; GitHub Actions supports this through OpenID Connect. Where the customer forbids outside pipelines from touching their cluster, use a pull model: a GitOps controller inside the cluster watches a repository and applies changes, so nothing reaches in from outside.
body.heading: Build once, promote through their gates

subtopics.title: CI/CD across the vendor and customer boundary

body.body: AWS Lambda runs code without provisioning servers, scales with request volume and bills for compute time used, which suits webhook handlers, document-triggered ingestion steps and glue between customer systems. LLM workloads strain the model in specific ways: a function has a maximum execution time, so a long agent loop or a slow model call can be cut off; time spent waiting on a model response is billed; cold starts add latency to interactive paths; and streaming responses need a supported invocation mode. A common split is functions for event-driven edges and short tool calls, and containers or a durable workflow engine for long-running agent runs. Check the customer's concurrency quotas and whether functions must attach to a private network, since both change behavior.
body.heading: Strengths and limits

subtopics.title: Serverless delivery and where it fits LLM systems

body.body: The twelve-factor rule is that configuration, meaning everything likely to vary between deploys, lives in the environment and not in the code. The test is whether the codebase could be made public without leaking a credential. For multi-customer delivery this is the mechanism that lets one image serve every customer: model endpoint, model name, database address, feature flags and tenant identifiers are all injected at deploy time. Avoid named environment groups baked into code such as a per-customer settings file; they multiply with every deployment. Secrets come from the customer's secret manager through workload identity, mounted or fetched at start. Validate configuration at startup and fail fast with a clear message, because a person on the customer's team, not you, may be reading the log.
body.heading: One artifact, many environments

subtopics.title: Configuration and secrets per customer environment

concepts.summary: Containers, pipelines and serverless functions are the packaging and delivery mechanics behind every customer deployment. The forward deployed twist is that the registry, the cluster and the pipeline often belong to someone else, so artifacts must be portable, configurable from outside, and promotable through a process you do not control. This lesson focuses on those constraints rather than on the basics of each tool.
concepts.title: Containers, CI/CD and serverless delivery

concepts.in_practice: A team keeps a connectivity matrix for each deployment: every source, destination, port and protocol, with the reason. They test the release in an internal environment that has no internet route and default-deny network policies, which catches most surprises before the customer sees them. For disconnected customers the pipeline emits an offline bundle with checksums alongside the normal release, and the installer reads every registry and endpoint address from configuration. A support bundle command and a written runbook stand in for the remote access the team will not have.

sources.title: Kubernetes: Services, Load Balancing, and Networking

body.body: A virtual private cloud is a logically isolated network with subnets, route tables, gateways and security groups. In a customer environment you rarely design it; you are handed subnets and must discover the rules. Ask which subnets have a route to the internet, whether egress passes through a proxy or firewall with an allowlist, how DNS resolves internal names, and how much address space is free, since pod networking can exhaust small ranges quickly.
body.heading: Reading the customer's network before you deploy

subtopics.title: Private network layout for a customer deployment

body.body: AWS PrivateLink lets resources in a VPC connect privately to supported AWS services, to services hosted in other accounts, and to partner services, as if they were inside the VPC, without an internet gateway, NAT device or public address. The consumer creates an interface endpoint, which appears as network interfaces with private addresses in their subnets; the provider exposes an endpoint service, typically fronted by a network load balancer. Traffic is one-directional by design: the consumer initiates, and the provider cannot reach back into the consumer network. That property makes it easier to get approved than peering, which joins two networks at the routing level and requires non-overlapping address ranges. Google Cloud Private Service Connect and Azure Private Link follow the same model.
body.heading: Reaching services without the public internet

body.body: Use private endpoints for cloud services the workload calls, including storage, the container registry, the secret store and the hosted model service, so the deployment works in subnets with no internet route. Use an endpoint service when the vendor control plane must be reachable from the customer network or the reverse. Use site-to-site VPN or a dedicated circuit when the workload must reach systems in a customer data center. List every outbound destination in the design document, with protocol and port, because that list becomes the firewall change request.
body.heading: Choosing a pattern

subtopics.title: Private connectivity: endpoints, peering and VPN

body.body: The Kubernetes network model gives every pod its own cluster-wide address, and pods can reach each other without address translation unless something restricts them. Services provide a stable address and DNS name in front of a changing set of pods; Ingress and the newer Gateway API expose HTTP routes to clients outside the cluster. NetworkPolicy objects restrict traffic by pod labels, namespaces and address ranges, but only take effect if the cluster's network plugin enforces them. Restricted customers often apply a default-deny policy per namespace, so your chart must ship explicit policies for every flow it needs: application to database, application to model endpoint, DNS, and metrics scraping. A missing DNS egress rule is the classic first failure, and it shows up as timeouts rather than refusals.
body.heading: Services, ingress and policy

subtopics.title: Kubernetes networking and egress control

body.body: An air-gapped environment has no route to the internet, so nothing can be pulled at install or run time. The release becomes a self-contained bundle: all container images exported as archives, charts, operating system packages, language dependencies, model weights and tokenizer files, plus checksums and signatures. The bundle is transferred through an approved process, scanned, and loaded into an internal registry and artifact store. Hunt down hidden network calls before shipping: telemetry, license checks, libraries that download model files on first use, and fonts or scripts loaded by a web front end from a public network.
body.heading: Everything arrives as a bundle

body.body: Hosted model APIs are unavailable, so inference runs on local GPUs with an open-weight model, and evaluation results from a hosted model do not transfer; rerun the evaluation suite on the model that will actually serve. You cannot attach a debugger or read dashboards remotely, so build a diagnostics command that collects logs, configuration and versions into a single redacted file the customer can review and hand back. Upgrades are infrequent and expensive, which raises the bar on installer idempotence, rollback and written runbooks.
body.heading: Operating without reaching in

subtopics.title: Air-gapped delivery

body.body: AWS GovCloud (US) consists of isolated regions designed for United States government agencies and customers with sensitive workloads and regulatory requirements. Accounts and credentials are separate from standard regions, resource names use a different partition, endpoints differ, and not every service or feature is available or arrives at the same time. Practically, hard-coded partitions, region names and endpoints in infrastructure code break, and a managed service you depend on may be missing, including specific hosted models. Parameterize partition and endpoints, and check service availability during scoping rather than at install.
body.heading: What a government region changes

body.body: Classified environments add physical and personnel constraints on top of air-gapping: work happens on site in accredited facilities by cleared staff, no personal devices or outside connectivity are allowed, and software enters through a formal review and transfer process. The system needs an authorization to operate, which rests on documented security controls. Expect slow iteration loops, so invest in a faithful unclassified replica environment where the installer and upgrade path are rehearsed end to end before each visit.
body.heading: Classified networks

subtopics.title: Government regions and classified environments

concepts.summary: Many enterprise and government customers run workloads on networks with no public ingress, tightly filtered egress, or no internet connection at all. This lesson covers private connectivity patterns, network controls inside Kubernetes, and what changes when the environment is air-gapped or in a government region. The recurring theme is that every dependency you normally fetch at run time must be either reachable privately or carried in.
concepts.title: Networking for private, air-gapped and classified customer environments

concepts.in_practice: A team first confirms the hardware the customer actually has, then picks a model and precision that fit its memory with headroom for the context lengths the use case needs. They install the GPU Operator or validate the existing driver setup, deploy the inference server as a Deployment on a tainted GPU node pool with weights loaded from an internal store, and expose it only inside the cluster behind an OpenAI-compatible interface. Load tests with realistic prompt and output lengths set the concurrency limit, and GPU utilization, memory, queue depth and time to first token are scraped into the customer's monitoring. The evaluation suite is rerun against the self-hosted model before anyone promises quality.

sources.title: NVIDIA GPU Operator: Time-Slicing GPUs in Kubernetes

body.body: A container does not see a GPU by default. The host needs the NVIDIA driver; the NVIDIA Container Toolkit then configures the container runtime, such as containerd or Docker, so that a container started with a GPU request gets the device files and driver libraries mounted in. On Kubernetes a device plugin advertises the GPUs on each node to the scheduler as an extended resource. Version alignment across driver, toolkit, CUDA libraries in the image and the framework is a frequent cause of failed starts, so record the versions you tested.
body.heading: Layers between the card and the container

body.body: The NVIDIA GPU Operator uses the Kubernetes operator pattern to manage all of that software as cluster components: the driver as a container, the container toolkit, the device plugin, node labeling through GPU feature discovery, and monitoring through a DCGM-based exporter. It is installed with Helm and lets GPU nodes run the same base operating system image as CPU nodes, since nothing is preinstalled by hand. In customer clusters, check first whether drivers are already baked into node images, in which case the operator is configured not to deploy its own. In disconnected environments every operator image must be mirrored to the internal registry beforehand.
body.heading: What the GPU Operator automates

subtopics.title: The GPU node stack: drivers, container toolkit, operator

body.body: Pods request GPUs through a vendor resource name such as nvidia.com/gpu, set under resource limits. GPUs are specified in limits; if a request is also given it must equal the limit. By default the count is a whole number, devices are not overcommitted, and a container cannot ask for a fraction of one. Nodes carry labels describing the GPU model and memory, added by node feature discovery, so workloads can use node selectors or affinity to land on the right hardware. GPU node pools are normally tainted so ordinary pods stay off them, and inference pods carry the matching toleration. Because nodes are expensive and slow to provision, plan for image pull time and model load time when designing autoscaling and readiness probes.
body.heading: Extended resources and their rules

subtopics.title: Scheduling GPUs in Kubernetes

body.body: Loading a model in a script handles one request at a time. A serving engine schedules many concurrent requests onto the GPU. vLLM is a high-throughput, memory-efficient inference and serving engine for LLMs; its core techniques are continuous batching, where new requests join the running batch at each generation step instead of waiting for a batch to finish, and efficient management of attention key-value memory through PagedAttention. It exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server, so application code written against a hosted API can be pointed at it by changing the base address and model name. It also supports streaming, quantized weights, and tool calling and structured output for models that have suitable chat templates.
body.heading: What a serving engine adds

body.body: Hugging Face Text Generation Inference is a toolkit for deploying and serving LLMs with token streaming, continuous batching, quantization options, and production features such as Prometheus metrics and distributed tracing. Selection in practice depends on which engine supports the customer's approved model and hardware, how well it handles your structured output and tool calling needs, and what the customer platform team is willing to operate. Whichever you choose, put it behind the same client interface as hosted models, and rerun your evaluation suite: a smaller open-weight model will behave differently on prompts tuned for a frontier model.
body.heading: Text Generation Inference and choosing

subtopics.title: Inference servers: vLLM and Text Generation Inference

body.body: GPU memory decides whether a model fits: the weights at the chosen precision, plus the key-value cache that grows with context length and the number of concurrent sequences. Quantization reduces the weight footprint at some quality cost that you must measure. Throughput is then tuned through maximum context length, concurrency limits and batch behavior. Measure time to first token, tokens per second per request and total tokens per second under realistic concurrency, since batching raises total throughput while slowing each individual stream.
body.heading: Memory first, then throughput

body.body: The GPU Operator supports time-slicing, which advertises each physical GPU as several replicas so multiple pods can be scheduled onto it and take turns. This is oversubscription: there is no memory isolation or fault isolation between the pods, so one workload can exhaust memory for the others. It suits development, embedding models and light workloads. Where isolation matters, hardware partitioning through Multi-Instance GPU on supported cards provides dedicated memory and compute slices. Large generation models generally get dedicated GPUs.
body.heading: Sharing a GPU

subtopics.title: Sizing, sharing and measuring GPU capacity

concepts.summary: When a customer cannot or will not call a hosted model API, the forward deployed engineer has to run open-weight models on GPUs inside the customer environment. This lesson covers how GPUs are exposed to containers and scheduled in Kubernetes, what an inference server does, and how to size and share scarce accelerators. The aim is to stand up and reason about a serving stack, not to train models.
concepts.title: GPU infrastructure and model serving for inference workloads

diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  REQ[Incoming request] --> Q{Tenant quota and criticality}
  Q -->|over quota or low priority under load| SHED[Reject early or queue]
  Q -->|admitted| R{Router}
  R -->|simple step| SMALL[Small fast model]
  R -->|hard step| LARGE[Large model with cached prefix]
  R -->|not urgent| BATCH[Batch interface]
  SMALL --> M[Usage record: tokens, cache, latency, tenant]
  LARGE --> M
  BATCH --> M
  M --> COST[Cost per outcome dashboard]

concepts.in_practice: A team instruments every model call with token counts, cache hits, latency and a tenant label before optimizing anything, then looks at where time and money actually go. Typical first moves are restructuring prompts so the stable prefix caches, moving bulk and evaluation work to batch, routing easy steps to a smaller model, and removing an agent turn. They set per-tenant quotas and a single retry layer with backoff and a budget, and define what the product does when capacity runs out. Each change is checked against the evaluation suite so a cost win does not hide a quality loss, and the result is reported to the customer as cost per business outcome.

body.body: Output generation dominates response time, because tokens are produced one at a time, while input tokens are processed far faster. The practical levers follow from that: generate fewer tokens by asking for concise or structured output; use a smaller or faster model for steps that do not need the strongest one; trim input where it is large enough to matter; make fewer sequential requests by combining steps; and run independent steps in parallel. Not every step needs a model at all; a lookup, a rule or a classical classifier is faster and cheaper where it is good enough.
body.heading: A short list of levers

body.body: Users judge responsiveness by time to first visible progress, not total time. Streaming tokens, showing which step an agent is on, and returning a partial result early all make a long operation acceptable without changing compute. Measure time to first token and total time separately, at the median and at the tail, and split them by stage: retrieval, each model call, each tool call. In agent systems the number of turns is usually the largest factor, so cutting one unnecessary round trip often beats any model-level optimization.
body.heading: Perceived latency

subtopics.title: Where latency comes from and how to cut it

body.body: Prompt caching lets a provider reuse the processed form of a prompt prefix across requests. With the Claude API you mark cache breakpoints, the prefix up to that point is stored, and later requests with an identical prefix read it at a fraction of the normal input price and with lower latency; writing the cache costs somewhat more than a normal input token, and entries expire after a short lifetime that is refreshed on each use. The design consequence is ordering: put stable content first (tool definitions, system instructions, reference documents, few-shot examples) and volatile content last. Anything that changes per request near the top, such as a timestamp or user name, invalidates everything after it. Track cache read and cache write token counts in the response usage to confirm it works.
body.heading: Prompt caching

body.body: Work that does not need an immediate answer, such as backfills, bulk classification, document enrichment and evaluation runs, can go through an asynchronous batch interface. With the Claude Message Batches API you submit many requests at once, each with your own identifier, poll until processing ends, then fetch results and match them by identifier; batches are priced at a substantial discount to standard calls and most complete well within the stated processing window. Batch requests do not consume the interactive path's capacity in the same way, which keeps overnight jobs from starving daytime users. Results can arrive in any order and individual requests can fail independently, so the consumer must be idempotent and handle partial success.
body.heading: Batch processing

subtopics.title: Prompt caching and batch processing

body.body: Hosted model providers limit requests and tokens per minute, and a self-hosted server is limited by GPU memory and batch capacity. Either way, a traffic spike or a few very large prompts can exhaust capacity. The guidance from large-scale service practice applies directly: reject excess load early and cheaply rather than accepting work you cannot finish; give each customer or tenant a quota so one cannot starve the rest; and classify requests by criticality so interactive user traffic is served before background jobs when capacity is short.
body.heading: Limits are in tokens, not only requests

body.body: Naive retries turn a brief overload into a sustained one. Use exponential backoff with jitter, honor any retry-after hint from the provider, and cap retries with a budget, for example a small ratio of retries to requests per client, so retries cannot multiply load. Retry at one layer only; when every layer of an agent stack retries, attempts multiply. Client-side throttling goes further: when a client sees a high share of its recent requests rejected, it starts dropping requests locally before sending them. Pair this with degradation paths: a smaller model, a cached answer, a shorter context, or a queued response.
body.heading: Retries without amplification

subtopics.title: Overload, rate limits and graceful degradation

body.body: Beyond hard caps on spend, a customer deployment needs a unit cost the buyer understands: cost per resolved ticket, per processed document, per agent run. Record input, output and cached tokens per call with tenant, feature and model labels, and join them to outcomes. The cloud cost optimization guidance applies as written: establish ownership, measure usage, match supply to demand, and revisit choices as prices and models change. Model routing, with a cheap model first and escalation on low confidence, is usually the largest single saving.
body.heading: From spend caps to cost per outcome

subtopics.title: Cost attribution and unit economics

concepts.summary: LLM systems have an unusual cost and latency profile: spend scales with tokens, latency scales mostly with output length, and capacity is bounded by provider rate limits or by GPUs. This lesson covers the levers that move latency and cost, the provider features built for it, and how to behave under overload. The skill is choosing a point on the quality, latency and cost surface that the customer can defend.
concepts.title: Scaling and performance-cost tradeoffs for LLM systems

modules.intro: This module covers how an AI forward deployed engineer gets a system running inside infrastructure the customer owns: their cloud accounts, their clusters, their private networks and sometimes their GPUs. It moves from cloud and delivery fundamentals to restricted networks, self-hosted inference, and the latency and cost tradeoffs that decide whether a deployment survives production.
modules.title: Infrastructure and Deployment into Customer Environments

from opentelemetry import trace

tracer = trace.get_tracer("support-agent")

def call_model(client, model, messages):
    with tracer.start_as_current_span(f"chat {model}") as span:
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.operation.name", "chat")
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", model)
        resp = client.chat(model=model, messages=messages)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.input_tokens", resp.usage.input_tokens)
        span.set_attribute("gen_ai.usage.output_tokens", resp.usage.output_tokens)

concepts.in_practice: A team instruments the agent service and its tools with OpenTelemetry SDKs and sends everything over OTLP to a collector that the deployment owns. The collector redacts sensitive attributes, applies tail sampling and fans out to the customer's chosen backends, which are often already in place and not negotiable. Before go-live the team builds one dashboard per deployment with the golden signals plus token cost and tool error rate, defines a small number of symptom-based alerts with a runbook each, and checks that a single request id from the customer's application can be followed through the agent trace into backend logs. During the pilot, engineers review sampled traces weekly to find slow steps, repeated loops and failing tools, and feed those findings into prompt, tool and evaluation changes.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry: Semantic conventions for generative AI systems
Google SRE Book: Monitoring Distributed Systems

body.body: Telemetry comes in three main signals. Logs are timestamped records of discrete events, most useful when structured as key-value fields and stamped with a trace id. Metrics are numeric measurements aggregated over time, cheap to store and well suited to dashboards and alerts. Traces record the path of one request through many services as a tree of spans. A system is observable when these signals let you answer questions you did not anticipate without shipping new code. In a deployment, the first task is to make all three share identifiers such as service name, environment, customer tenant and trace id, so that you can pivot from an alert to a trace to the exact log lines.
body.heading: Logs, metrics and traces

body.body: The four golden signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Measure latency for successful and failed requests separately, and look at percentiles rather than averages, because a slow tail hides inside a healthy mean. Page a human only for symptoms that users feel and that need action now; send cause-level signals, such as a full disk on one node, to dashboards or tickets. Every page should be urgent, actionable and novel. For an AI feature, add signals the classic list misses: tokens per request, cost per task, tool-call error rate, and the rate of refusals or schema-invalid outputs.
body.heading: What to alert on

subtopics.title: The three signals and what to alert on

body.body: A trace is a set of spans that share a trace id; each span has a name, start and end time, attributes, events, a status and a parent span id. Context propagation carries the trace id and parent span id across process boundaries, usually in the W3C traceparent header. In field work the hard part is the boundaries you do not own: message queues, batch jobs, customer gateways that strip headers, and vendor APIs. Carry context in message metadata, use span links for fan-in from batches, and record the customer's own correlation id as a span attribute so that both sides can search for the same request.
body.heading: Spans, context and where propagation breaks

subtopics.title: Distributed tracing and context propagation

body.body: OpenTelemetry publishes semantic conventions for generative AI so that model calls look the same regardless of provider or framework. They cover spans for model inference, embeddings, tool execution and agent invocation, plus metrics such as token usage and operation duration, and events for inputs and outputs. Typical attributes include gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.response.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and gen_ai.usage.output_tokens. The conventions are still evolving, so pin the version your instrumentation emits and expect attribute names to change between releases. Using them means a backend can compute cost and latency per model without custom parsing.
body.heading: What the conventions define

body.body: One agent run should be one trace. The root span is the task or user turn; under it sit a span per model call, a span per tool execution, and spans for retrieval and guardrail checks. Tool spans in turn parent the ordinary HTTP and database spans of the systems they touch, which is what joins agent behavior to backend behavior. Add attributes that make runs comparable: prompt version, agent name, step index, retry count and finish reason. With that shape you can answer the questions that matter in a pilot: which step is slow, which tool fails, where the loop repeated, and what a task costs.
body.heading: Shape of an agent trace

subtopics.title: Agent traces and the GenAI semantic conventions

body.body: Prompts and completions are the most useful debugging data and the most sensitive. They can contain personal data, credentials pasted by users, and customer documents. Instrumentation libraries generally leave content capture off by default and require an explicit opt-in. Decide per environment: full content in development, redacted or hashed content in production, with a short retention period and access limited to the people on call. Run redaction in the collector pipeline rather than in each service, so that one policy applies everywhere, and check where the telemetry backend stores data, because a customer's residency rules apply to traces as much as to databases.
body.heading: Content capture is a data decision

body.body: Agent traces are large; a single run can produce hundreds of spans and long payloads. Head sampling decides at the start of a trace and is cheap; tail sampling decides after the trace completes, so you can keep every error, every slow run and every run with a guardrail hit while keeping a small share of normal ones. Keep metric labels low in cardinality: model, operation and tenant tier are fine, user id and prompt text are not. Put high-cardinality detail on spans and logs instead.
body.heading: Sampling and cardinality

subtopics.title: Prompt content, privacy and telemetry cost

concepts.summary: Observability is the ability to understand what a running system is doing from the telemetry it emits: logs, metrics and traces. For AI deployments the same signals are extended with spans for model calls, tool executions and agent steps, so that cost, latency and behavior can be explained per task. This lesson covers the signals, what to alert on, how agent traces are shaped, and how to handle sensitive prompt content in telemetry.
concepts.title: Observability: logs, metrics and agent traces

diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  A[Problem report] --> B[Triage and mitigate]
  B --> C[Examine telemetry]
  C --> D[Form hypothesis]
  D --> E[Test hypothesis]
  E -->|not confirmed| C
  E -->|confirmed| F[Fix and verify]
  F --> G[Postmortem and action items]
  G --> H[Regression test or eval case]

concepts.in_practice: When a customer reports a problem, the engineer on the account first confirms impact and mitigates, often by turning off a feature flag or rolling back the last release, and opens a shared incident channel with the customer's technical contact. They pull the trace for a failing request id, compare it with a healthy one, and bisect across hops until the fault is isolated to their service, the customer's infrastructure or a model or tool behavior. Notes go into a running incident document as they work. After resolution the team writes a postmortem within a few days, reviews it in a short meeting, files action items in the normal backlog with owners, adds the failing case to the test or evaluation suite, and sends the customer a plain summary of what happened and what changed.

body.body: Effective troubleshooting is the hypothetico-deductive method applied to a running system. Start from a problem report that states expected behavior, actual behavior and how to reproduce it. Triage first: in a major outage the priority is to stop the bleeding by rolling back, shifting traffic or disabling a feature, not to find the root cause. Then examine the telemetry, form a hypothesis, and test it either by comparing observed state with what the hypothesis predicts or by changing one thing and watching the result. Write down what you tried and what you saw, so that the next person does not repeat it.
body.heading: Triage, examine, diagnose, test

body.body: Two techniques cut most problems down quickly. Bisection splits the data path in half: check whether the output is correct midway through the pipeline, then repeat in the faulty half. Asking what changed last works because a running system tends to keep working until a deploy, config push, data change or load shift disturbs it. Avoid the common traps: chasing symptoms that are unrelated, treating correlation as cause, and favoring an exotic explanation when a recent change is the simpler one. A negative result is still a result; record it.
body.heading: Narrowing the search

subtopics.title: A systematic troubleshooting loop

body.body: In a customer deployment half the system is not yours. You may have no shell access, logs may sit in the customer's tools, and the failing component may be a gateway, an identity provider or a legacy database owned by another team. Prepare for that before the incident: agree on a shared correlation id that appears in both sides' logs, document who owns each hop, and build a small diagnostic script that checks connectivity, credentials, versions and clock skew from inside the customer network. When something fails, ask for specific evidence, such as the request id, a timestamp with time zone and the response body, rather than a general description.
body.heading: Working with partial access

body.body: Reproduce the request at each boundary. Replay the same payload against your API directly, then through the customer's proxy, then from the customer application. The hop where behavior changes is where the fault lives. Typical causes in restricted environments are TLS inspection that rewrites certificates, proxies that buffer or cut streaming responses, allowlists that miss a new endpoint, expired tokens, and payload size limits. Keep a minimal reproduction that the customer's team can run themselves; it turns a debate about ownership into a shared test with a clear result.
body.heading: Isolating whose side the fault is on

subtopics.title: Debugging across the customer boundary

body.body: A wrong agent output is a symptom with several possible layers of cause: missing or stale context from retrieval, a tool that returned an error or an unexpected shape, a prompt change, a model version change, truncation at the context limit, or plain sampling variance. Open the trace for the run and read it step by step: what the model was shown, what it called, what came back. Most failures turn out to be context or tool problems rather than model reasoning problems. Check whether the failure is stable by rerunning the same inputs several times; a failure that appears one time in ten needs a rate, not a single anecdote.
body.heading: From a bad answer to a cause

body.body: Once the cause is known, capture the failing input as a regression case in the evaluation set before changing anything, confirm that it fails, apply the fix, and confirm that it passes without breaking other cases. Record model id, prompt version and tool versions with every run, so that a later regression can be traced to a specific change. Fixes that only edit the prompt for one example tend to break others, which is why the full suite must rerun after each change.
body.heading: Closing the loop

subtopics.title: Debugging LLM and agent failures

body.body: A postmortem is a written record of an incident: its impact, the timeline, the actions taken to mitigate it, the root causes and contributing factors, and the follow-up actions to prevent recurrence. Teams define triggers in advance, such as user-visible downtime above a threshold, any data loss, a manual on-call intervention like a rollback, or a monitoring failure where a human found the problem before an alert did. Write it while memory is fresh, and include what went well and where the team got lucky, because luck is a risk that has not been paid for yet.
body.heading: What a postmortem contains

body.body: Blameless means the document assumes that everyone acted with good intent on the information available, and it looks for the conditions that made the mistake possible instead of naming a person. That keeps people willing to report problems. A postmortem is only finished when it has been reviewed and its action items have an owner, a priority and a tracked ticket. For customer-facing incidents, a separate external summary states impact, cause and remediation in plain language and without internal detail. Share completed postmortems widely so that other deployments learn from them.
body.heading: Blameless and followed through

subtopics.title: Blameless postmortems and follow-through

concepts.summary: Debugging production systems is a disciplined loop of triage, observation, hypothesis and test, not a hunt driven by intuition. In customer deployments the loop has to work across systems you do not own and across non-deterministic model behavior. When an incident is over, a blameless postmortem turns it into tracked improvements.
concepts.title: Debugging production systems and running postmortems

concepts.in_practice: At scoping, the engineer asks which regulations and internal frameworks apply and who signs off, then drafts a data flow diagram that marks every trust boundary, including the hop to the model provider. The team runs a short threat modeling session with the customer's security architect, ranks the threats, and records mitigations as design requirements: a dedicated least-privilege identity for the agent, approval gates on writes, redaction before egress, and audit logging. They fill in the security questionnaire from a maintained evidence pack, map their controls to the customer's framework, and agree on a shared responsibility matrix. Findings from the review become tracked tickets, exceptions are signed with an expiry date, and the same documents are updated whenever a new tool, data source or model is added.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5: Security and Privacy Controls

body.body: Threat modeling is a structured way to find what can go wrong before an attacker does. The OWASP process has three steps: decompose the application, determine and rank threats, and determine countermeasures and mitigations. Decomposition produces data flow diagrams that show external entities, processes, data stores, data flows and the trust boundaries between them, plus a list of entry points, assets and trust levels. Threats are then enumerated per element, commonly with STRIDE: spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege. Each threat is ranked by risk and mapped to a control or an accepted risk.
body.heading: The process

body.body: An AI deployment adds trust boundaries that classic models miss. Any text the model reads, including retrieved documents, emails, tickets and tool results, is untrusted input that may carry instructions, so prompt injection belongs in the tampering and elevation columns. The model's tool permissions define the blast radius: model the agent as a principal with its own least-privilege identity, not as the user. Add the model provider as an external entity with its own data flow, and record what is sent, what is retained and for how long. Mitigations are architectural: scoped credentials, human approval for writes, output validation and egress limits.
body.heading: What changes with a model in the flow

subtopics.title: Threat modeling an AI deployment

body.body: The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard is a catalog of testable security requirements for web applications and services, grouped into chapters such as authentication, session management, access control, input validation, cryptography, logging and API security. It defines three verification levels of increasing rigor, so a team can pick the level that matches the sensitivity of the application and use the requirements as a checklist in design and review. For a forward deployed engineer it is a practical way to answer the question of whether the application is secure with specific, verifiable statements rather than assurances.
body.heading: ASVS for application requirements

body.body: NIST SP 800-53 Revision 5 is a catalog of security and privacy controls for information systems and organizations, organized into families such as access control, audit and accountability, identification and authentication, incident response, system and communications protection, and supply chain risk management. Government customers and many regulated enterprises use it, or baselines derived from it, as the reference in security reviews. You rarely implement a family alone; instead you map what your deployment does to the control ids the customer cares about, and note which controls are inherited from the cloud provider, which are the customer's and which are yours.
body.heading: NIST SP 800-53 for organizational controls

subtopics.title: Control frameworks: ASVS and NIST SP 800-53

body.body: Beyond encrypting data in transit and at rest and masking it outside production, the strongest move in a regulated deployment is to shrink what is in scope. Tokenize card data so that only a payment processor handles the real number, send the model only the fields a task needs, and redact identifiers before text leaves the customer boundary. Treat the model provider as a subprocessor: confirm its retention terms, whether data is used for training, and whether a business associate agreement or equivalent contract is required for health data.
body.heading: Reducing scope before adding controls

subtopics.title: Protecting PII and payment data: encryption and masking

body.body: Data governance answers who may use which data, for what purpose and for how long. In an AI deployment the same record can end up in several derived places: a prompt, an embedding index, a cache, a trace and an evaluation set. Keep an inventory of those copies with a classification, an owner and a retention period for each. A deletion or access request must reach every one of them, so store source record ids alongside chunks and embeddings to make targeted deletion possible. Enforce document-level permissions at retrieval time, so that the model never sees a document that the asking user could not open.
body.heading: Governing data that flows through AI systems

subtopics.title: Governance: retention, deletion and access for derived data

body.body: Enterprise customers gate deployment on a security review. Expect a questionnaire, an architecture and data flow diagram, a list of subprocessors, penetration test results, and evidence of controls such as single sign-on, role-based access, audit logging, encryption, backup and incident response. Sector rules add specifics: health data brings HIPAA safeguards, card data brings PCI DSS, and contact center work brings consent rules for call recording and outbound contact. Prepare a reusable evidence pack and a shared responsibility matrix that states for each control whether the vendor, the customer or the cloud provider operates it.
body.heading: What reviewers ask for

body.body: Reviews go faster when the design removes questions. Deploy inside the customer's cloud account or network when data may not leave it, use their identity provider, keep secrets in their vault, and write an immutable audit log of every agent action with who, what, when and on whose behalf. Raise the review at scoping time, not the week before launch; approvals in regulated firms often take longer than the build. Record every accepted risk and exception in writing with an owner and an expiry date.
body.heading: Designing so the review is short

subtopics.title: Getting through a customer security review

concepts.summary: Regulated customers will not put an AI system into production until it passes their security and compliance review. This lesson covers how to threat model a deployment, how the common control frameworks are used, how to protect and govern regulated data as it flows through prompts and indexes, and how to design and document a deployment so that the review goes quickly.
concepts.title: Security reviews, governance and compliance in regulated industries

concepts.in_practice: After each engagement the team holds a short review that lists what was built, what was reused and what was painful, and tags candidates for extraction. When the same need has shown up at several customers, a field engineer and a platform engineer pair for a sprint or two to pull the core into the product behind a per-tenant toggle, with customer specifics moved into configuration. The first customer is migrated to the shared version to prove it, then ownership moves to the platform team and the capability is published as a template and a catalog entry in the developer portal. Product managers use the engagement log and adoption numbers to decide what gets generalized next, and release toggles are removed once all tenants are on the new path.

body.body: Forward deployed work produces custom code by design, and most of it should stay custom. The signal for reuse is repetition: when a second or third customer needs the same connector, evaluation harness or deployment script, the pattern is real and its variation points are visible. Generalizing after one build tends to encode that customer's quirks as product assumptions. Keep a running log of what each engagement built, what was copied from a previous one and what had to be changed; that log is the evidence the product team needs to prioritize.
body.heading: From one customer to a pattern

body.body: To extract a feature, split it into a stable core, a set of declared extension points and per-customer configuration. Field mappings, prompts, thresholds and credentials belong in configuration; orchestration, retries, auth flows and telemetry belong in the core. Write the contract first: inputs, outputs, error behavior and version policy. Then migrate the original customer onto the extracted version, since a reusable component that its first user does not run is unproven. Hand over ownership explicitly, with docs, tests and an on-call owner.
body.heading: Separating core from configuration

subtopics.title: Deciding what to generalize

body.body: Feature toggles let one codebase behave differently without a branch or a fork per customer. Fowler's taxonomy sorts them by lifetime and dynamism. Release toggles hide unfinished code on trunk and should live days or weeks. Experiment toggles route cohorts for A/B tests. Ops toggles act as kill switches for risky or costly behavior, such as an expensive model path. Permission toggles enable features for specific users or tenants and can live for years. Each category deserves different handling: a long-lived permission toggle needs proper management, while a release toggle needs a removal date.
body.heading: Toggle categories

body.body: Avoid scattering conditionals on a flag name through the code. Put the decision behind a toggle router, expose a named feature decision such as whether to include a step, and where the variation is large inject a different strategy implementation at construction time. Toggle configuration ranges from static files that ship with a deploy to a dynamic store that changes per request. Toggles carry a cost: every one multiplies the states to test, so test the expected production configuration plus the fallback, keep an inventory with owners, and delete release toggles once the rollout completes.
body.heading: Keeping toggles manageable

subtopics.title: Feature toggles for per-customer variation

body.body: Team Topologies describes four team types: stream-aligned teams that deliver along a flow of work, enabling teams that help others gain capabilities, complicated-subsystem teams that own areas needing deep specialist knowledge, and platform teams that provide internal services to speed up stream-aligned teams. They interact in three modes: collaboration, X-as-a-Service and facilitating. A forward deployed team is stream-aligned to a customer. It collaborates closely with the platform team while a capability is being discovered, then shifts to consuming it as a service once the interface is stable. The aim throughout is to reduce cognitive load on delivery teams.
body.heading: Team types and interaction modes

body.body: Platform engineering treats internal tooling as a product with users, a roadmap and adoption metrics. The platform offers self-service capabilities so that an engineer can provision an environment, deploy an agent or add a connector without filing a ticket. Keep it as thin as possible: the smallest set of APIs, templates and docs that removes real friction. Measure it by time to first deployment for a new customer, the share of engagements using the paved path, and how often teams work around it. Adoption should be earned by usefulness, not mandated.
body.heading: Platform as a product

subtopics.title: Platform as a product and team interaction

body.body: An internal developer portal gives one place to find and create software. Backstage, an open source framework for building such portals, centers on a software catalog that tracks ownership and metadata for services, libraries, pipelines and other components; software templates that scaffold a new project with the organization's standards already applied; and TechDocs, which builds documentation from Markdown kept beside the code. Plugins extend it to show CI status, cloud resources or cost. For field teams, a template that creates a new customer deployment with auth, telemetry, evaluation and CI wired in is the highest-value golden path.
body.heading: Catalog, templates and docs

body.body: The best internal tools start as a script someone wrote during an engagement: a data profiler, a connectivity checker, a trace viewer, an onboarding checklist. Promote one when several engineers are copying it. Give it a home in a shared repository, a command-line entry point, versioned releases and a short document that states what it does and what it does not. Feed the same pain points into onboarding flows and docs, since each question asked twice by a customer or a new engineer points to a gap.
body.heading: Tooling built from field pain

subtopics.title: Developer portals, golden paths and field tooling

concepts.summary: Forward deployed work creates custom solutions under time pressure, and its long-term value depends on how much of that work the next engagement can reuse. This lesson covers how to decide what to generalize, how feature toggles let one codebase serve many customers, how field teams and platform teams work together, and how developer portals and internal tools turn repeated work into paved paths.
concepts.title: Turning one-off customer builds into reusable platform features and internal tooling

It closes with how to turn the custom work of one engagement into platform features and internal tools that the next engagement can reuse.
